title: SQL
intro:
At TikTok, Google, Samsung and similar companies the SQL round is usually 30 to 45 minutes with 2 to 4 questions that get harder, written in a shared editor (CoderPad, HackerRank, a Google Doc) and often **not executed**. They grade correct logic, clean structure, edge cases (NULLs, ties, duplicates) and how you explain your plan out loud.
How to use this tab: read [How to approach a SQL question](#sql-exam-approach) first, then the section of the day's focus topic before you open `2_sql.ipynb`. All examples use one small short-video app schema (`users`, `videos`, `views`), and every query and result table was run in SQLite.
When a hint says "Learn more: sql-top-n", come back here. For the pandas version of each pattern see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and the [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas); for a one-page syntax list see the [SQL cheat sheet](#cheat-sql).

sections.title: How to approach a SQL exam question
sections.summary: A 6-step routine for every SQL question, plus the running example schema used in this tab.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Every SQL question, from the first easy filter to the last hard window query. The routine matters most when you cannot run the code: in a shared doc your only test is your own reasoning.

### The running example schema (used in every section of this tab)
A small short-video app. Memorize the shape once; all later examples use the same rows.

- `users(user_id, username, country, signup_date)`: one row per user. `eli` has a NULL country. `fay` never watched anything.
- `videos(video_id, creator_id, category, upload_date, duration_sec)`: one row per video. `creator_id` is a `user_id`. Video 15 has no views.
- `views(view_id, user_id, video_id, view_ts, watch_sec)`: one row per view event. View 12 has NULL `watch_sec` (a logging bug).

`users`

| user_id | username | country | signup_date |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | KR | 2024-01-03 |
| 2 | ben | US | 2024-01-10 |
| 3 | chen | CN | 2024-02-01 |
| 4 | dana | US | 2024-02-15 |
| 5 | eli | NULL | 2024-03-01 |
| 6 | fay | KR | 2024-03-05 |

`videos`

| video_id | creator_id | category | upload_date | duration_sec |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1 | dance | 2024-01-05 | 30 |
| 11 | 1 | comedy | 2024-01-20 | 45 |
| 12 | 2 | dance | 2024-02-02 | 60 |
| 13 | 3 | food | 2024-02-10 | 20 |
| 14 | 3 | dance | 2024-02-20 | 15 |
| 15 | 4 | comedy | 2024-03-02 | 50 |

`views`

| view_id | user_id | video_id | view_ts | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 10 | 2024-03-01 09:00:00 | 24 |
| 2 | 3 | 10 | 2024-03-01 10:30:00 | 12 |
| 3 | 4 | 10 | 2024-03-02 20:15:00 | 30 |
| 4 | 1 | 12 | 2024-03-02 21:00:00 | 55 |
| 5 | 3 | 12 | 2024-03-03 08:00:00 | 25 |
| 6 | 2 | 11 | 2024-03-03 12:00:00 | 40 |
| 7 | 5 | 13 | 2024-03-04 18:00:00 | 20 |
| 8 | 2 | 13 | 2024-03-05 19:30:00 | 5 |
| 9 | 4 | 14 | 2024-03-05 22:00:00 | 15 |
| 10 | 1 | 14 | 2024-03-06 07:45:00 | 9 |
| 11 | 2 | 12 | 2024-03-06 23:10:00 | 60 |
| 12 | 3 | 11 | 2024-03-07 13:00:00 | NULL |
| 13 | 2 | 10 | 2024-03-07 21:00:00 | 30 |

Dates are stored as text `'YYYY-MM-DD'` and timestamps as `'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'`, which is how SQLite works. In PostgreSQL or BigQuery they would be `DATE` and `TIMESTAMP` columns (see [Dates and times](#sql-dates)).

### The 6-step routine
| Step | What you do | What you say out loud |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Clarify | Ask about the grain of each table, duplicates, NULLs, ties, time zone, what "active" means | "Is `views` one row per view event? Can a user view the same video twice?" |
| 2. Define the output | Write the output columns and the grain of one result row | "One row per country, with the number of distinct viewers." |
| 3. Plan in steps | Break the problem into 2 to 4 named steps (each becomes a CTE) | "First I filter March views, then join users, then count distinct users per country." |
| 4. Write | Write the query top to bottom, one CTE per step | Narrate each step briefly. |
| 5. Check | Walk 2 or 3 rows through the query by hand. Check NULLs, ties, empty groups, duplicates from joins | "A user with no views would disappear in an inner join. Is that what we want?" |
| 6. Extend | Mention performance and follow-ups | "On a big table I would filter by date first, because it is probably partitioned by date." |

### Worked example 1: a full walk-through
**Question:** "For each country, how many distinct users watched at least one video in March 2024?"

1. Clarify: count users, not views, so `COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)`. Users with NULL country: keep them as their own group (say this out loud).
2. Output: `country, viewers`, one row per country.
3. Plan: March views, join to users, group by country.
4. Write:

```sql
SELECT u.country,
       COUNT(DISTINCT v.user_id) AS viewers
FROM views AS v
JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = v.user_id
WHERE v.view_ts >= '2024-03-01' AND v.view_ts < '2024-04-01'
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY viewers DESC, u.country;
```

Result:

| country | viewers |
|---|---|
| US | 2 |
| NULL | 1 |
| CN | 1 |
| KR | 1 |

5. Check: `ben` has 5 views but counts once in US, so DISTINCT works. `eli` forms the NULL group. `fay` has no views and correctly does not appear. The NULL country sorts first in SQLite and MySQL but last in PostgreSQL ascending order; if the order matters, say so.

### Worked example 2: turning a vague question into a precise one
**Question:** "Which creator is the most popular?"

Popular could mean views, total watch time, or distinct viewers. Pick one, say why, and offer the others. Here: total watch seconds of the creator's videos.

```sql
WITH creator_watch AS (
    SELECT vd.creator_id,
           SUM(v.watch_sec) AS total_watch_sec,
           COUNT(*)         AS n_views
    FROM views AS v
    JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.creator_id
)
SELECT c.creator_id, u.username, c.total_watch_sec, c.n_views
FROM creator_watch AS c
JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = c.creator_id
ORDER BY c.total_watch_sec DESC;
```

Result:

| creator_id | username | total_watch_sec | n_views |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | ben | 140 | 3 |
| 1 | ana | 136 | 6 |
| 3 | chen | 49 | 4 |

Creator 2 (`ben`) wins on watch time, but creator 1 (`ana`) has more views. This is exactly the point to raise: the choice of metric changes the answer. Creator 4 has no views and is missing; if the question was "rank all creators", you need a LEFT JOIN (see [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls)).

### Exam angle
- Examiners at big tech often give a product story ("TikTok wants to know which videos keep users watching") and expect you to translate it into tables, grain and metric. Clarifying questions are scored, not a waste of time.
- Typical follow-ups: "What if there are ties?", "What if a user has no events?", "How would this run on 10 billion rows?", "How would you do it in pandas?".
- A strong opening sounds like: "Before I write anything: `views` is one row per event, so if I need users I will count distinct user ids. I will build it in three CTEs."

### Traps
- Writing before you know the grain. Most wrong answers come from counting rows when the question asks for users.
- Forgetting rows that should appear with 0 (inner join drops them).
- Silent duplicates after a join (fan-out), see [Joins](#sql-joins).
- Not stating assumptions. If you assume "no duplicate events", say it.
- Spending 10 minutes on one detail. Write a working version first, then improve.

### Complexity and performance (what to say)
- Filter early (`WHERE` on the partition column, usually a date) so less data is scanned and joined.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` is expensive on huge tables; BigQuery offers `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`.
- Joins on indexed or partitioned keys are cheap; a join that multiplies rows is the most common performance and correctness bug.

### Practice and links
- Used every day; the timed mock exams on days 7, 14, 21 and 28 test this routine under pressure.
- Next: [Logical query order](#sql-query-order), [SQL basics](#sql-basics). Same habit for coding questions: [How to recognize the pattern](#algo-recognize). For product framing of metrics: [Product metrics](#stats-product-metrics).
- External: [LeetCode Top SQL 50](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-sql-50/), [Mode SQL tutorial](https://mode.com/sql-tutorial/), [SQLite SQL reference](https://www.sqlite.org/lang.html).

sections.title: Logical query order
sections.summary: Why an alias or window function is not visible in WHERE: SQL runs clauses in a different order than you write them.
sections.body:
### When to use it
- You get an error like "column does not exist" for an alias you just defined.
- You want to filter on an aggregate (use `HAVING`) or on a window function (use an outer query).
- You are unsure whether a condition belongs in `WHERE`, `HAVING`, or the `ON` of a join.

### Core idea
You write SQL in the order `SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT`, but the database evaluates it in a different logical order. Each step only sees what earlier steps produced. So `WHERE` cannot use a `SELECT` alias or an aggregate, because `SELECT` and `GROUP BY` have not happened yet. `ORDER BY` runs after `SELECT`, so it can use aliases.

| Order | Clause | What it does | Can it see SELECT aliases? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `FROM`, `JOIN ... ON` | Builds the row set | No |
| 2 | `WHERE` | Filters single rows | No (SQLite allows it as an extension; do not rely on it) |
| 3 | `GROUP BY` | Forms groups | No in standard SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL and BigQuery allow it) |
| 4 | `HAVING` | Filters groups, can use aggregates | No in standard SQL |
| 5 | `SELECT` | Computes columns, aliases, aggregates | Defines them |
| 6 | Window functions | Computed on the result after grouping | They are part of SELECT |
| 7 | `DISTINCT` | Removes duplicate output rows | Yes |
| 8 | `ORDER BY` | Sorts | Yes |
| 9 | `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` / `FETCH` | Cuts rows | Yes |

BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks and DuckDB add `QUALIFY` after window functions: a `WHERE` for window results (see [Top N per group](#sql-top-n)).

### Template
```sql
SELECT   group_col, AGG(x) AS metric      -- 5
FROM     t                                -- 1
WHERE    row_level_condition              -- 2
GROUP BY group_col                        -- 3
HAVING   AGG(x) > threshold               -- 4
ORDER BY metric DESC                      -- 8 (alias is fine here)
LIMIT    10;                              -- 9
```

### Worked example 1: WHERE vs HAVING
**Question:** "Categories with more than one video uploaded in 2024."

`WHERE COUNT(*) > 1` fails: when `WHERE` runs, no groups exist yet. SQLite says "misuse of aggregate". The row filter goes in `WHERE`, the group filter in `HAVING`:

```sql
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n_videos
FROM videos
WHERE upload_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY n_videos DESC;
```

Result:

| category | n_videos |
|---|---|
| dance | 3 |
| comedy | 2 |

`food` has only one video and is removed by `HAVING`.

### Worked example 2: filtering on a window function
**Question:** "The longest view (by `watch_sec`) of each user."

This fails, because `rn` is computed in step 6 and `WHERE` runs in step 2:
```sql
-- ERROR: window function result is not available in WHERE
SELECT user_id, view_id, watch_sec,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY watch_sec DESC) AS rn
FROM views
WHERE rn = 1;
```
Fix: compute it in a CTE (or subquery), filter outside.

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT user_id, view_id, watch_sec,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                              ORDER BY watch_sec DESC, view_id) AS rn
    FROM views
)
SELECT user_id, view_id, watch_sec
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | view_id | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 55 |
| 2 | 11 | 60 |
| 3 | 5 | 25 |
| 4 | 3 | 30 |
| 5 | 7 | 20 |

`view_id` is a tie breaker: if a user had two equally long views, the result would still be deterministic. Watch user 3: view 12 has NULL `watch_sec`. SQLite and MySQL sort NULL as the smallest value, so it comes last with `DESC`. PostgreSQL sorts NULL as the largest value, so with `DESC` it would come first and user 3 would get view 12. Write `ORDER BY watch_sec DESC NULLS LAST` in PostgreSQL. In BigQuery you can write the whole query in one step with `QUALIFY rn = 1`.

### Worked example 3: alias in ORDER BY is fine
```sql
SELECT video_id, SUM(watch_sec) AS total_watch
FROM views
GROUP BY video_id
ORDER BY total_watch DESC
LIMIT 3;
```

Result:

| video_id | total_watch |
|---|---|
| 12 | 140 |
| 10 | 96 |
| 11 | 40 |

### Exam angle
- A classic warm-up: "What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?" Model answer: "WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. If a condition does not need an aggregate, put it in WHERE, because it removes rows earlier and is cheaper."
- Follow-up: "Why can't I use the alias in WHERE?" Answer with the logical order above.
- Follow-up: "Where does a condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN go?" In `ON` if you want to keep unmatched rows; see [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls).

### Traps
- Putting a non-aggregate filter in `HAVING`. It works but scans more data; examiners notice.
- Relying on SQLite allowing aliases in `WHERE`. It breaks in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and BigQuery.
- Thinking `LIMIT` runs before `ORDER BY`. It runs last, so `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 3` gives the true top 3.
- `DISTINCT` runs after window functions, so `SELECT DISTINCT user_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)` does not deduplicate what you expect.

### Performance
The logical order is not the physical plan: the optimizer may push filters down. But writing filters in `WHERE` (not `HAVING`) and filtering before joins makes your intent clear and helps the optimizer.

### Practice and links
- Underlies every day; especially days 2 (aggregation), 10 (window ranking) and 11 (top N).
- Related: [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation), [Window functions: ranking](#sql-window-ranking), [Top N per group](#sql-top-n), [Subqueries](#sql-subqueries). pandas has the same ideas in a different order: filter, `groupby`, `agg`, then filter again ([SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents)).
- External: [SQLite SELECT](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_select.html), [PostgreSQL SELECT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html), [BigQuery QUALIFY](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax#qualify_clause).

sections.title: SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, NULL
sections.summary: Filtering and sorting rows, and the NULL rules that make easy questions tricky.
sections.body:
### When to use it
"List", "find all", "show the users who", "which videos are longer than": anything that filters and sorts rows without grouping. Easy questions in the first minutes of a round test exactly this, and the points are lost on NULLs.

### Core idea
`SELECT` picks columns, `FROM` picks the table, `WHERE` keeps rows where the condition is TRUE, `ORDER BY` sorts, `LIMIT` cuts. SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, and `WHERE` keeps only TRUE rows. So `country <> 'US'` silently drops users whose country is NULL.

### Template
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT col_a, col_b * 2 AS doubled       -- DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows
FROM   t
WHERE  col_c IN ('x', 'y')                        -- list membership
  AND  col_d BETWEEN 10 AND 20                    -- inclusive on both ends
  AND  col_e LIKE 'da%'                           -- % any text, _ one character
  AND  (col_f IS NULL OR col_f <> 'z')            -- NULL needs IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY col_a ASC, doubled DESC
LIMIT 10;                                         -- OFFSET 20 to skip rows
```

### Worked example 1: the NULL trap
**Question:** "Users not from the US."

```sql
SELECT user_id, username, country
FROM users
WHERE country <> 'US';
```

Result:

| user_id | username | country |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | KR |
| 3 | chen | CN |
| 6 | fay | KR |

`eli` (country NULL) is missing, because `NULL <> 'US'` is UNKNOWN. If "not from the US" should include unknown countries:

```sql
SELECT user_id, username, COALESCE(country, 'unknown') AS country
FROM users
WHERE country <> 'US' OR country IS NULL;
```

Result:

| user_id | username | country |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | KR |
| 3 | chen | CN |
| 5 | eli | unknown |
| 6 | fay | KR |

`COALESCE(a, b)` returns the first non-NULL argument. It is the standard way to replace NULLs for display or for math (`COALESCE(watch_sec, 0)`).

### Worked example 2: filter, compute, sort
**Question:** "Views in which the user watched at least 80 percent of the video, longest first."

```sql
SELECT v.view_id, v.video_id, v.watch_sec, vd.duration_sec,
       ROUND(1.0 * v.watch_sec / vd.duration_sec, 2) AS completion
FROM views AS v
JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
WHERE 1.0 * v.watch_sec / vd.duration_sec >= 0.8
ORDER BY completion DESC, v.view_id;
```

Result:

| view_id | video_id | watch_sec | duration_sec | completion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 10 | 30 | 30 | 1.0 |
| 7 | 13 | 20 | 20 | 1.0 |
| 9 | 14 | 15 | 15 | 1.0 |
| 11 | 12 | 60 | 60 | 1.0 |
| 13 | 10 | 30 | 30 | 1.0 |
| 4 | 12 | 55 | 60 | 0.92 |
| 6 | 11 | 40 | 45 | 0.89 |
| 1 | 10 | 24 | 30 | 0.8 |

Two details: `1.0 *` forces decimal division (in SQLite and PostgreSQL `30 / 45` is `0` because both are integers), and view 12 (NULL `watch_sec`) drops out because NULL compared to 0.8 is UNKNOWN.

### Worked example 3: AND / OR precedence
**Question:** "Dance or comedy videos longer than 40 seconds."

```sql
SELECT video_id, category, duration_sec
FROM videos
WHERE category IN ('dance', 'comedy')
  AND duration_sec > 40;
```

Result:

| video_id | category | duration_sec |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | comedy | 45 |
| 12 | dance | 60 |
| 15 | comedy | 50 |

The wrong version `WHERE category = 'dance' OR category = 'comedy' AND duration_sec > 40` returns every dance video, because `AND` binds tighter than `OR`. Use `IN` or parentheses.

### Dialect notes: limiting rows
| Dialect | First 3 rows |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, BigQuery, DuckDB | `ORDER BY x LIMIT 3` |
| SQL Server | `SELECT TOP 3 ... ORDER BY x` |
| Standard SQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle 12c+, SQL Server | `ORDER BY x OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY` |

Other small differences: string concatenation is `||` in PostgreSQL, SQLite and BigQuery but `CONCAT()` in MySQL. `LIKE` is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL (use `ILIKE`) but case-insensitive for ASCII in SQLite and MySQL (default collation).

### NULL rules to remember
| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `NULL = NULL` | UNKNOWN (use `IS NULL`) |
| `NULL + 5` | NULL |
| `COUNT(col)`, `SUM`, `AVG` | ignore NULLs |
| `NOT IN (list containing NULL)` | never TRUE, returns no rows |
| `ORDER BY col` | NULLs first in SQLite/MySQL, last in PostgreSQL (ascending). Use `NULLS LAST` where supported |

### Exam angle
- Easy questions are asked to check speed and care. Read the prompt for "including", "excluding", "unknown". Then say: "There are NULL countries; I will treat them as not US and include them" or ask.
- Follow-up: "Why did your count drop by one?" Answer: the NULL comparison.

### Traps
- `= NULL` instead of `IS NULL` (always returns no rows).
- Integer division, especially when computing rates.
- `BETWEEN` on timestamps: `BETWEEN '2024-03-01' AND '2024-03-07'` misses everything on March 7 after midnight. Use a half-open range `>= '2024-03-01' AND < '2024-03-08'` (see [Dates](#sql-dates)).
- `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns arbitrary rows.
- `SELECT DISTINCT` to hide duplicates you do not understand. Find the cause instead.

### Complexity
A filter on an indexed or partitioned column avoids a full scan. `LIKE 'abc%'` can use an index, `LIKE '%abc'` cannot. Sorting is `O(n log n)`; `ORDER BY ... LIMIT k` can use a top-k heap, like [Heap](#algo-heap).

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 1, reviewed on days 2 and 7.
- Related: [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation), [CASE WHEN](#sql-case-when), [pandas boolean filtering](#sql-pandas-equivalents), [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- External: [LeetCode 584 Find Customer Referee (NULL trap)](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-customer-referee/), [LeetCode 1757 Recyclable and Low Fat Products](https://leetcode.com/problems/recyclable-and-low-fat-products/), [LeetCode 595 Big Countries](https://leetcode.com/problems/big-countries/), [SQLBolt](https://sqlbolt.com/).

sections.title: Aggregation: GROUP BY, COUNT, SUM, AVG, HAVING
sections.summary: Collapse rows into one row per group; know exactly what COUNT and AVG do with NULLs and duplicates.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "per", "for each", "by", "total", "average", "how many", "at least N". The output has fewer rows than the input, one per group. If the output must keep every input row and add a group value next to it, you need a window function instead ([Window functions](#sql-window-ranking)).

### Core idea
`GROUP BY` splits rows into groups by the listed columns; each aggregate returns one value per group. Every column in `SELECT` must be either in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate (MySQL with an old setting and SQLite accept other columns and return an arbitrary value; never rely on that). Aggregates ignore NULLs, except `COUNT(*)`, which counts rows. The single most important question is the grain: what is one row of the input, and what should one row of the output be?

| Function | Counts or uses | NULLs |
|---|---|---|
| `COUNT(*)` | all rows | counted |
| `COUNT(col)` | rows where col is not NULL | skipped |
| `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` | distinct non-NULL values | skipped |
| `SUM(col)`, `MIN`, `MAX` | non-NULL values | skipped; all NULL gives NULL (not 0) |
| `AVG(col)` | `SUM(col) / COUNT(col)` | skipped, so the denominator shrinks |

### Template
```sql
SELECT group_col,
       COUNT(*)                 AS n_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)  AS n_users,
       SUM(x)                   AS total_x,
       AVG(x)                   AS avg_x          -- NULLs excluded
FROM   t
WHERE  row_filter
GROUP BY group_col
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2                            -- filter on groups
ORDER BY n_rows DESC;
```

### Worked example 1: the five counts
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                          AS n_views,
       COUNT(watch_sec)                  AS n_with_watch,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)           AS n_viewers,
       SUM(watch_sec)                    AS total_watch,
       ROUND(AVG(watch_sec), 2)          AS avg_watch_ignore_null,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(watch_sec, 0)), 2) AS avg_watch_null_as_0
FROM views;
```

Result:

| n_views | n_with_watch | n_viewers | total_watch | avg_watch_ignore_null | avg_watch_null_as_0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | 12 | 5 | 325 | 27.08 | 25.0 |

13 view rows, but only 12 have a watch time. `AVG` divides by 12, the `COALESCE` version divides by 13. Which one is right is a product question: is the NULL a missing log (ignore it) or a real zero-second view (count it as 0)? Say this in the exam.

### Worked example 2: per-group metrics with HAVING
**Question:** "For each video with at least 2 views: number of views, distinct viewers and average watch seconds."

```sql
SELECT video_id,
       COUNT(*)                 AS n_views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)  AS n_viewers,
       ROUND(AVG(watch_sec), 1) AS avg_watch
FROM views
GROUP BY video_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY n_views DESC, video_id;
```

Result:

| video_id | n_views | n_viewers | avg_watch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 4 | 3 | 24.0 |
| 12 | 3 | 3 | 46.7 |
| 11 | 2 | 2 | 40.0 |
| 13 | 2 | 2 | 12.5 |
| 14 | 2 | 2 | 12.0 |

Check by hand: video 10 has 4 views but only 3 viewers, because `ben` watched it twice (views 1 and 13). Video 11 has 2 views but `avg_watch` uses only one value (view 12 is NULL).

### Worked example 3: aggregate of an aggregate
**Question:** "On average, how many views does a viewer make?"

You cannot nest `AVG(COUNT(*))` in most dialects. Two options: aggregate in two steps, or divide two totals.

```sql
WITH per_user AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n_views
    FROM views
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(n_views), 2) AS avg_views_per_viewer,
       MAX(n_views)           AS max_views
FROM per_user;
```

Result:

| avg_views_per_viewer | max_views |
|---|---|
| 2.6 | 5 |

Same answer as `1.0 * COUNT(*) / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` = 13 / 5 = 2.6. Note the denominator: users with 0 views (`fay`) are not included. "Per viewer" and "per user" are different metrics. For "per user" you need a LEFT JOIN from `users` ([LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls)), giving 13 / 6 = 2.17.

### Dialect notes
- Integer division: `SUM(a) / COUNT(*)` is integer division in PostgreSQL, SQLite and SQL Server if both are integers. MySQL and BigQuery `/` return decimals. Write `1.0 * SUM(a) / COUNT(*)` or `CAST(... AS FLOAT)`; BigQuery also has `SAFE_DIVIDE(a, b)` (NULL instead of a division-by-zero error).
- `AVG` of an integer column in PostgreSQL returns numeric, in SQLite a float. Use `ROUND(x, 2)`.
- PostgreSQL has `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)`; everywhere else use `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` ([CASE WHEN](#sql-case-when)).
- Approximate distinct counts on big data: `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` (BigQuery, Spark), `approx_distinct` (Presto/Trino).

### Exam angle
- Expect "per user", "per day", "per creator" variants of the same question. State the grain first: "views is one row per event, I need one row per video".
- Follow-ups: "What happens with NULL watch time?", "Why is your average higher than mine?" (different denominators), "Find users with more than 3 views" (HAVING).
- Strong sentence: "COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs, and COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values, so I use COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) because the question asks for users."

### Traps
- `COUNT(*)` when the question says users or videos: you count events instead of entities.
- `SUM` of an all-NULL group is NULL, not 0. Wrap with `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)`.
- Selecting a non-grouped column. Errors in PostgreSQL and BigQuery; silently wrong in SQLite and permissive MySQL.
- Averaging averages: the mean of per-day averages is not the overall average when days have different counts. See [Ratios](#sql-ratios) and [Ratio metrics](#stats-ratio-metrics).
- Aggregating after a join that duplicated rows (fan-out), see [Joins](#sql-joins).

### Complexity
`GROUP BY` is a hash aggregation, `O(n)` time and memory proportional to the number of groups (like a Python dict, see [Hashing](#algo-hashing)), or a sort, `O(n log n)`. `COUNT(DISTINCT)` needs a set per group, which is the expensive part on big data.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 2, reviewed on days 3, 5 and 7.
- Related: [CASE WHEN for conditional counts](#sql-case-when), [Window functions keep every row](#sql-window-ranking). pandas: `df.groupby('video_id').agg(n=('view_id','size'), users=('user_id','nunique'))`, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- External: [LeetCode 1683 Invalid Tweets](https://leetcode.com/problems/invalid-tweets/), [LeetCode 1141 User Activity for the Past 30 Days I](https://leetcode.com/problems/user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i/), [LeetCode 596 Classes More Than 5 Students](https://leetcode.com/problems/classes-more-than-5-students/), [PostgreSQL aggregate functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html).

sections.title: Joins and join cardinality
sections.summary: Combine tables on keys; predict how many rows a join returns, and avoid fan-out double counting.
sections.body:
### When to use it
The answer needs columns from more than one table: "views per category" (category lives in `videos`), "viewers by country" (country lives in `users`). Before writing a join, answer two questions: which key connects the tables, and is the relationship one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many?

### Core idea
A join pairs each row of the left table with every row of the right table that matches the `ON` condition. If one video has 3 views, joining `videos` to `views` gives 3 rows for that video: this is correct for counting views, but it multiplies anything that belongs to the video (like `duration_sec`) when you sum it. This multiplication is called **fan-out** and it is the most common silent bug in SQL exams.

| Join | Keeps | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `INNER JOIN` (or `JOIN`) | only matching pairs | enrich events with attributes |
| `LEFT JOIN` | all left rows; NULLs where no match | keep users with zero events, anti-join |
| `RIGHT JOIN` | all right rows | rarely used; rewrite as LEFT JOIN |
| `FULL OUTER JOIN` | all rows of both sides | reconcile two sources (not in MySQL; SQLite since 3.39) |
| `CROSS JOIN` | every pair | build a grid: all users x all dates |
| self join | table joined to itself | pairs, previous event, see [Self join](#sql-self-join) |

Row count rule for `A JOIN B ON A.k = B.k`: for each key, (rows in A with k) x (rows in B with k), summed over keys.

### Template
```sql
SELECT a.col, b.col
FROM   table_a AS a
JOIN   table_b AS b
       ON  b.a_id = a.id             -- the key
       AND b.date >= a.start_date    -- optional extra conditions
LEFT JOIN table_c AS c ON c.id = b.c_id;
```

### Worked example 1: enrich events, then group
**Question:** "Total watch seconds and number of views per category."

```sql
SELECT vd.category,
       COUNT(*)          AS n_views,
       SUM(v.watch_sec)  AS total_watch
FROM views AS v
JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
GROUP BY vd.category
ORDER BY total_watch DESC;
```

Result:

| category | n_views | total_watch |
|---|---|---|
| dance | 9 | 260 |
| comedy | 2 | 40 |
| food | 2 | 25 |

`views` to `videos` is many-to-one, so every view row appears exactly once: safe to count and sum view columns.

### Worked example 2: the fan-out trap
**Question:** "For each creator: total duration of uploaded videos and total number of views."

Wrong: join first, then sum a video-level column.

```sql
SELECT vd.creator_id,
       SUM(vd.duration_sec) AS total_duration_WRONG,
       COUNT(v.view_id)     AS n_views
FROM videos AS vd
LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.video_id = vd.video_id
GROUP BY vd.creator_id
ORDER BY vd.creator_id;
```

Result:

| creator_id | total_duration_WRONG | n_views |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 210 | 6 |
| 2 | 180 | 3 |
| 3 | 70 | 4 |
| 4 | 50 | 0 |

Creator 1 uploaded 30 + 45 = 75 seconds of video, not 210: video 10 (4 views) is counted 4 times and video 11 (2 views) twice. Right: aggregate each table to the creator grain first, then join one-to-one.

```sql
WITH dur AS (
    SELECT creator_id, SUM(duration_sec) AS total_duration
    FROM videos
    GROUP BY creator_id
),
vw AS (
    SELECT vd.creator_id, COUNT(*) AS n_views
    FROM views AS v
    JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.creator_id
)
SELECT d.creator_id, d.total_duration, COALESCE(vw.n_views, 0) AS n_views
FROM dur AS d
LEFT JOIN vw ON vw.creator_id = d.creator_id
ORDER BY d.creator_id;
```

Result:

| creator_id | total_duration | n_views |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 75 | 6 |
| 2 | 60 | 3 |
| 3 | 35 | 4 |
| 4 | 50 | 0 |

### Worked example 3: predict the row count
```sql
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u JOIN views v ON v.user_id = u.user_id)      AS inner_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u LEFT JOIN views v ON v.user_id = u.user_id) AS left_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users u CROSS JOIN videos vd)                       AS cross_rows;
```

Result:

| inner_rows | left_rows | cross_rows |
|---|---|---|
| 13 | 14 | 36 |

Inner: each of the 13 views has a user. Left: 13 plus one row for `fay`, who has no views. Cross: 6 users x 6 videos = 36. Saying these numbers before running the query shows you understand the join.

### Exam angle
- "Why did your total go up after the join?" is a standard follow-up. Answer: "The join is one-to-many, so the video-level column repeats once per view. I aggregate before joining, or I sum only columns at the many side."
- Many-to-many joins (two event tables on `user_id`) explode rows: 100 views x 50 likes for a user becomes 5,000 rows. Aggregate each to the user grain first.
- Be ready to name the join algorithm: hash join (build a hash table on the smaller side, `O(n + m)`), sort-merge join, nested loop with an index. In Spark/BigQuery, a small table is broadcast to all workers.

### Traps
- Fan-out (above). Check: does `COUNT(*)` after the join equal `COUNT(*)` of the many-side table?
- Joining on the wrong key: `videos.creator_id` is a user, `views.user_id` is a viewer. Different roles of the same id type.
- Inner join silently drops rows with no match, including keys with NULL (NULL never equals NULL).
- Ambiguous column names: always use table aliases (`v.user_id`).
- `COUNT(DISTINCT)` as a patch for fan-out hides the bug and still breaks `SUM`.

### Complexity
Hash join `O(n + m)` time, memory for the smaller side. Fan-out output can be `O(n x m)` per key; on big data the size of the output, not the input, is what kills a query. Filter and aggregate before joining.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 3, reviewed on days 4, 7 and 9.
- Related: [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls), [Self join](#sql-self-join), [CTEs to aggregate before joining](#sql-cte). pandas: `views.merge(videos, on='video_id', how='left', validate='many_to_one')` catches fan-out, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents). The hash join is the same idea as [Hashing](#algo-hashing).
- External: [LeetCode 1378 Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier](https://leetcode.com/problems/replace-employee-id-with-the-unique-identifier/), [LeetCode 1068 Product Sales Analysis I](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-sales-analysis-i/), [LeetCode 1280 Students and Examinations](https://leetcode.com/problems/students-and-examinations/), [PostgreSQL joins tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-join.html).

sections.title: LEFT JOIN, NULLs and anti-joins
sections.summary: Keep entities with zero activity, find rows with no match, and put filters in ON vs WHERE correctly.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "including users with no views", "show 0 for", "never", "did not", "without any", "all creators". Whenever the driving entity (users, videos, dates) must appear even with no activity, start from that entity table and LEFT JOIN the events.

### Core idea
`LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table. Where nothing matches, all columns from the right table are NULL. Three consequences follow. First, filter on the right table in `ON`, not in `WHERE`, or you remove the NULL rows and turn it back into an inner join. Second, count a right-table column (`COUNT(v.view_id)`), not `COUNT(*)`, so unmatched rows count as 0. Third, `WHERE right.key IS NULL` keeps only unmatched rows: this is an **anti-join** ("never", "did not").

### Template
```sql
-- every user with their activity (0 if none)
SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(v.view_id) AS n_views, COALESCE(SUM(v.watch_sec), 0) AS watch
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v
       ON v.user_id = u.user_id
      AND v.view_ts >= '2024-03-05'        -- right-table filter goes in ON
GROUP BY u.user_id;

-- anti-join: users with no views
SELECT u.user_id FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE v.view_id IS NULL;                   -- test a column that is never NULL when matched
```

### Worked example 1: anti-join
**Question:** "Users who never watched a video." Two equivalent forms:

```sql
SELECT u.user_id, u.username
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE v.view_id IS NULL;
```

Result:

| user_id | username |
|---|---|
| 6 | fay |

```sql
SELECT u.user_id, u.username
FROM users AS u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM views AS v WHERE v.user_id = u.user_id);
```

Result:

| user_id | username |
|---|---|
| 6 | fay |

Test the right table's primary key (`v.view_id`), not a column that can be NULL on its own, like `v.watch_sec`. With `watch_sec IS NULL` you would also return `chen`, because view 12 has a NULL watch time.

### Worked example 2: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) after a LEFT JOIN
```sql
SELECT u.username,
       COUNT(*)         AS count_star_WRONG,
       COUNT(v.view_id) AS n_views
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| username | count_star_WRONG | n_views |
|---|---|---|
| ana | 2 | 2 |
| ben | 5 | 5 |
| chen | 3 | 3 |
| dana | 2 | 2 |
| eli | 1 | 1 |
| fay | 1 | 0 |

`fay` has one row in the joined result (with NULLs), so `COUNT(*)` says 1. `COUNT(v.view_id)` correctly says 0.

### Worked example 3: filter in ON vs WHERE
**Question:** "Every user and their number of views from March 5 onward."

Filter in `WHERE` (wrong, drops users):

```sql
SELECT u.username, COUNT(v.view_id) AS n_views
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE v.view_ts >= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| username | n_views |
|---|---|
| ana | 1 |
| ben | 3 |
| chen | 1 |
| dana | 1 |

Filter in `ON` (right, keeps every user):

```sql
SELECT u.username, COUNT(v.view_id) AS n_views
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN views AS v
       ON v.user_id = u.user_id
      AND v.view_ts >= '2024-03-05'
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| username | n_views |
|---|---|
| ana | 1 |
| ben | 3 |
| chen | 1 |
| dana | 1 |
| eli | 0 |
| fay | 0 |

In the first query the `WHERE` runs after the join; `eli` only watched on March 4, and `fay` has a single joined row with NULL `view_ts` (NULL compared to a date is UNKNOWN). No row of theirs passes the `WHERE`, so they vanish. Rule: conditions on the left (driving) table go in `WHERE`, conditions on the right table go in `ON`.

### Worked example 4: the NOT IN NULL trap
**Question:** "Users whose country is not a country of anyone who signed up in March." March signups are `eli` (NULL) and `fay` (KR).

```sql
SELECT username FROM users
WHERE country NOT IN (SELECT country FROM users WHERE signup_date >= '2024-03-01');
```

Result:

| username |
|---|

No rows. The list contains NULL, so `country NOT IN ('KR', NULL)` means `country <> 'KR' AND country <> NULL`, and the second part is never TRUE. Use `NOT EXISTS`, which handles NULL safely:

```sql
SELECT u.username FROM users AS u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM users AS m
    WHERE m.signup_date >= '2024-03-01' AND m.country = u.country
);
```

Result:

| username |
|---|
| ben |
| chen |
| dana |
| eli |

`eli` is returned too, because NULL never equals anything. If unknown countries should be excluded, add `AND u.country IS NOT NULL` and say it.

### Exam angle
- LeetCode 183 "Customers Who Never Order" style questions are very common as the first question of a round.
- Follow-ups: "Make sure users with zero views show 0", "Why did the user disappear when you added the date filter?", "NOT IN or NOT EXISTS?". Model answer: "I prefer NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, because NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery has a NULL, and NOT EXISTS usually gets the same anti-join plan."
- For metrics like "average views per user", the denominator must include zero-activity users: start from `users`.

### Traps
- Right-table filter in `WHERE` (turns LEFT into INNER).
- `COUNT(*)` after LEFT JOIN (counts 1 for no activity).
- `SUM` on no match gives NULL: use `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)`.
- `NOT IN` with a nullable subquery column.
- A LEFT JOIN followed by an INNER JOIN to a third table on a right-side column removes the unmatched rows again. Make the later join a LEFT JOIN too.

### Complexity
The anti-join (`NOT EXISTS` or LEFT JOIN IS NULL) is a hash anti-join, `O(n + m)`. `NOT IN` can be much slower in some engines because of the NULL semantics.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 4, reviewed on days 5, 7 and 11.
- Related: [Joins](#sql-joins), [Subqueries: EXISTS](#sql-subqueries), [SQL basics: NULL rules](#sql-basics), [Retention](#sql-retention) (a LEFT JOIN from the cohort). pandas: `merge(how='left', indicator=True)` then filter `_merge == 'left_only'`, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- External: [LeetCode 183 Customers Who Never Order](https://leetcode.com/problems/customers-who-never-order/), [LeetCode 1581 Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions](https://leetcode.com/problems/customer-who-visited-but-did-not-make-any-transactions/), [LeetCode 577 Employee Bonus](https://leetcode.com/problems/employee-bonus/), [LeetCode 1934 Confirmation Rate](https://leetcode.com/problems/confirmation-rate/).

sections.title: CASE WHEN and conditional aggregation
sections.summary: If-then logic inside a query: bucket values, count only some rows, and build several metrics in one pass.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "bucket", "segment", "label as", "number of X and number of Y per", "share of views that", "rate", "percentage", one column per category. If you notice you want to run the same query twice with different `WHERE` filters, use conditional aggregation instead: one pass, one row per group, several metrics.

### Core idea
`CASE WHEN cond1 THEN a WHEN cond2 THEN b ELSE c END` returns the value of the first true condition, from top to bottom. Without `ELSE`, the result is NULL when nothing matches. Inside an aggregate it becomes a filter: `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts rows where the condition holds, and `AVG(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)` gives the share of rows where it holds. This is the most used SQL pattern for product metrics (rates, funnels, pivots).

### Template
```sql
SELECT group_col,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS n,
       SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)             AS n_cond,
       AVG(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)           AS share_cond,     -- 1.0, not 1
       SUM(CASE WHEN cat = 'a' THEN x ELSE 0 END)        AS x_in_a,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN cond THEN user_id END)   AS users_cond      -- no ELSE: NULL is skipped
FROM t
GROUP BY group_col;
```
PostgreSQL also has `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)`; BigQuery and MySQL have `IF(cond, a, b)`; SQL Server has `IIF`. `CASE` works everywhere.

### Worked example 1: bucketing (order of WHEN matters)
**Question:** "Classify each view by completion: full (at least 90 percent), partial (at least 50 percent), skip (below 50 percent). How many views are in each bucket?"

```sql
SELECT CASE
         WHEN v.watch_sec IS NULL                        THEN 'unknown'
         WHEN 1.0 * v.watch_sec / vd.duration_sec >= 0.9 THEN 'full'
         WHEN 1.0 * v.watch_sec / vd.duration_sec >= 0.5 THEN 'partial'
         ELSE 'skip'
       END AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS n_views
FROM views AS v
JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY n_views DESC, bucket;
```

Result:

| bucket | n_views |
|---|---|
| full | 6 |
| partial | 3 |
| skip | 3 |
| unknown | 1 |

Because `CASE` stops at the first true condition, the `partial` branch only sees views below 0.9, so you do not need `>= 0.5 AND < 0.9`. If you put `>= 0.5` first, every full view would be labelled partial. The explicit NULL branch keeps view 12 visible; without it, view 12 would fall into `ELSE 'skip'`, which is wrong.

### Worked example 2: several metrics per group in one pass
**Question:** "Per user: total views, views of dance videos, views of other categories, and the share of views that were full watches."

```sql
SELECT v.user_id,
       COUNT(*)                                                    AS n_views,
       SUM(CASE WHEN vd.category = 'dance' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)      AS dance_views,
       SUM(CASE WHEN vd.category <> 'dance' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS other_views,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN v.watch_sec >= 0.9 * vd.duration_sec
                      THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END), 2)                     AS full_watch_rate
FROM views AS v
JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
GROUP BY v.user_id
ORDER BY v.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | n_views | dance_views | other_views | full_watch_rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0.5 |
| 2 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 0.4 |
| 3 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0.0 |
| 4 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 1.0 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1.0 |

User 3 (`chen`): 3 views, none full. View 12 has NULL watch time, the condition is UNKNOWN, so `ELSE 0` applies and it counts as not full. If NULL views should be excluded from the denominator instead, use `ELSE NULL` for them (`AVG` skips NULLs). Decide and say which.

### Worked example 3: pivot rows into columns
**Question:** "One row per country, one column per category, values = views."

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(u.country, 'unknown')                         AS country,
       SUM(CASE WHEN vd.category = 'dance'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS dance,
       SUM(CASE WHEN vd.category = 'comedy' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS comedy,
       SUM(CASE WHEN vd.category = 'food'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS food
FROM views AS v
JOIN users  AS u  ON u.user_id  = v.user_id
JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
GROUP BY COALESCE(u.country, 'unknown')
ORDER BY country;
```

Result:

| country | dance | comedy | food |
|---|---|---|---|
| CN | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| KR | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| US | 5 | 1 | 1 |
| unknown | 0 | 0 | 1 |

This is a manual pivot. The categories must be known in advance; more on this in [Pivot](#sql-pivot).

### Exam angle
- Rate questions are everywhere at TikTok and Google: "completion rate per video", "share of users who did X", "click-through rate by day". Model answer: "I compute the numerator and the denominator in the same GROUP BY with a CASE inside SUM, then divide, casting to decimal."
- Follow-ups: "How do you handle NULL?", "Why `1.0` and not `1`?", "Can you give me both the count and the rate?".
- `CASE` in `ORDER BY` for a custom order: `ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'high' THEN 1 WHEN 'mid' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`.

### Traps
- Wrong order of `WHEN` branches (broad condition first).
- Missing `ELSE` inside `SUM`: the sum still works (NULLs skipped), but inside `AVG` a missing `ELSE 0` changes the denominator. Be deliberate.
- `AVG(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` is fine in SQLite and BigQuery, but in PostgreSQL integer inputs give a numeric result; with `SUM(...) / COUNT(*)` you get integer division. Use `1.0`.
- `CASE WHEN col = NULL` never matches. Use `WHEN col IS NULL`.
- Different result types in branches (`THEN 1 ELSE 'none'`) error in strict dialects.

### Complexity
One scan, `O(n)`, regardless of how many conditional columns you add. This is cheaper than several queries joined together or several `UNION ALL` branches.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 5, reviewed on days 6, 7 and 17 (funnels).
- Related: [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation), [Ratios and rates](#sql-ratios), [Funnels](#sql-funnels), [Pivot](#sql-pivot), [Ratio metrics in A/B tests](#stats-ratio-metrics). pandas: `np.where`, `np.select`, `pd.cut`, or `pivot_table`, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- External: [LeetCode 1193 Monthly Transactions I](https://leetcode.com/problems/monthly-transactions-i/), [LeetCode 1907 Count Salary Categories](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-salary-categories/), [LeetCode 1211 Queries Quality and Percentage](https://leetcode.com/problems/queries-quality-and-percentage/), [LeetCode 610 Triangle Judgement](https://leetcode.com/problems/triangle-judgement/).

sections.title: Subqueries: scalar, IN, EXISTS, correlated, derived tables
sections.summary: A query inside a query: compare to an overall or per-group value, test membership, or aggregate in two steps.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "above the average", "more than the overall", "users who have ever", "users who never", "the maximum of the totals". Any time you need a value that is computed from the data itself and then used as a filter or column.

### Core idea
There are four kinds, by where they sit and what they return.

| Kind | Where | Returns | Example use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scalar | `SELECT` or `WHERE` | one value | compare to the overall average |
| `IN` / `NOT IN` | `WHERE` | a list of values | users who watched dance |
| `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` | `WHERE` | true or false per outer row | ever / never questions |
| Correlated | anywhere | depends on the outer row | compare to the average of the same group |
| Derived table | `FROM` | a table (needs an alias) | aggregate twice |

A correlated subquery references a column of the outer query (`WHERE v2.video_id = v.video_id`), so logically it runs once per outer row. Modern optimizers often rewrite it as a join, but a window function or a CTE plus join is usually clearer.

### Template
```sql
-- scalar
SELECT * FROM t WHERE x > (SELECT AVG(x) FROM t);
-- membership
SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM views WHERE ...);
-- existence (safe with NULLs)
SELECT * FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM views v WHERE v.user_id = u.user_id);
-- derived table
SELECT AVG(n) FROM (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM views GROUP BY user_id) AS per_user;
```

### Worked example 1: scalar subquery
**Question:** "Views with watch time above the overall average watch time."

```sql
SELECT view_id, user_id, video_id, watch_sec
FROM views
WHERE watch_sec > (SELECT AVG(watch_sec) FROM views)
ORDER BY watch_sec DESC, view_id;
```

Result:

| view_id | user_id | video_id | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | 2 | 12 | 60 |
| 4 | 1 | 12 | 55 |
| 6 | 2 | 11 | 40 |
| 3 | 4 | 10 | 30 |
| 13 | 2 | 10 | 30 |

The overall average is about 27.08 (NULL view excluded), so views with 30 seconds or more qualify.

### Worked example 2: correlated subquery (compare to own group)
**Question:** "Views that are above the average watch time of the same video."

```sql
SELECT v.view_id, v.video_id, v.watch_sec
FROM views AS v
WHERE v.watch_sec > (
    SELECT AVG(v2.watch_sec)
    FROM views AS v2
    WHERE v2.video_id = v.video_id      -- correlation: same video as the outer row
)
ORDER BY v.video_id, v.view_id;
```

Result:

| view_id | video_id | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 10 | 30 |
| 13 | 10 | 30 |
| 4 | 12 | 55 |
| 11 | 12 | 60 |
| 7 | 13 | 20 |
| 9 | 14 | 15 |

Check video 10: watch times 24, 12, 30, 30, average 24, so only the two 30-second views pass. The same result with a window function, which most examiners prefer for big tables:

```sql
SELECT view_id, video_id, watch_sec
FROM (
    SELECT v.*, AVG(watch_sec) OVER (PARTITION BY video_id) AS video_avg
    FROM views AS v
) AS t
WHERE watch_sec > video_avg
ORDER BY video_id, view_id;
```

Result:

| view_id | video_id | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 10 | 30 |
| 13 | 10 | 30 |
| 4 | 12 | 55 |
| 11 | 12 | 60 |
| 7 | 13 | 20 |
| 9 | 14 | 15 |

### Worked example 3: IN and EXISTS
**Question:** "Users who watched at least one dance video."

```sql
SELECT u.user_id, u.username
FROM users AS u
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM views AS v
    JOIN videos AS vd ON vd.video_id = v.video_id
    WHERE v.user_id = u.user_id AND vd.category = 'dance'
)
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | username |
|---|---|
| 1 | ana |
| 2 | ben |
| 3 | chen |
| 4 | dana |

`WHERE u.user_id IN (SELECT v.user_id FROM views v JOIN videos vd ... WHERE vd.category = 'dance')` gives the same result. A plain `JOIN` would return `ben` twice (he has several dance views) unless you add `DISTINCT`; `IN` and `EXISTS` never duplicate the outer rows. For the negative version ("never watched dance") use `NOT EXISTS`, not `NOT IN`, because of the NULL trap explained in [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls).

### Worked example 4: derived table (aggregate twice)
**Question:** "The highest total watch time of any user, and who it is."

```sql
SELECT user_id, total_watch
FROM (
    SELECT user_id, SUM(watch_sec) AS total_watch
    FROM views
    GROUP BY user_id
) AS per_user
WHERE total_watch = (SELECT MAX(total_watch)
                     FROM (SELECT SUM(watch_sec) AS total_watch
                           FROM views GROUP BY user_id) AS t);
```

Result:

| user_id | total_watch |
|---|---|
| 2 | 159 |

It works, but the per-user aggregation is written twice. This is exactly the moment to switch to a CTE ([CTEs](#sql-cte)) or a ranking window function ([Top N](#sql-top-n)). Using `= MAX` returns all tied users, which is usually what "who" means.

### Exam angle
- "Find employees who earn more than their department average" (correlated subquery or window) and "second highest salary" (scalar subquery with `MAX ... WHERE < MAX`) are classic. See [Top N](#sql-top-n).
- Follow-up: "Can you rewrite this without a correlated subquery?" Answer with a window function (`AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`) or a CTE with a GROUP BY plus join.
- Model sentence: "I use EXISTS because I only need to know whether a match exists; it stops at the first match and cannot duplicate users."

### Traps
- A scalar subquery that returns more than one row: error in PostgreSQL ("more than one row returned"); SQLite silently takes the first row.
- A scalar subquery that returns no rows gives NULL, and `x > NULL` filters everything out.
- `NOT IN` with NULLs (returns nothing).
- Derived tables need an alias in PostgreSQL and MySQL (`AS t`).
- Deeply nested subqueries are hard to read under pressure. More than two levels: use CTEs.

### Complexity
Uncorrelated subqueries run once. A correlated subquery is logically `O(n x m)` (once per outer row); with an index on the correlation key or after the optimizer rewrites it to a join, it is close to `O(n + m)`. A window function does it in one sort per partition, `O(n log n)`.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 6, reviewed on days 7 and 8.
- Related: [CTEs](#sql-cte), [Window functions](#sql-window-ranking), [Top N and Nth highest](#sql-top-n), [LEFT JOIN anti-join](#sql-left-join-nulls). pandas: `df[df.x > df.x.mean()]`, and `groupby().transform('mean')` for the correlated version, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents).
- External: [LeetCode 1978 Employees Whose Manager Left the Company](https://leetcode.com/problems/employees-whose-manager-left-the-company/), [LeetCode 585 Investments in 2016](https://leetcode.com/problems/investments-in-2016/), [LeetCode 1164 Product Price at a Given Date](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-price-at-a-given-date/), [PostgreSQL subquery expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html).

sections.title: CTEs (WITH): write queries in named steps
sections.summary: Break a hard question into small named steps; the standard way to write readable exam SQL.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Almost every medium or hard question. Signals: the answer needs two levels of aggregation, the same intermediate result is used twice, or you can describe the solution as "first ..., then ..., then ...". Examiners read CTE code much faster than nested subqueries, and you can debug each step on its own.

### Core idea
`WITH name AS (query)` defines a temporary named result that exists only for this statement. Later CTEs and the final `SELECT` can use earlier ones, so you build a pipeline: filter, then aggregate, then join, then rank. Each step should have one clear grain (one row per user, per video, per day). Name CTEs by what one row is: `per_user`, `daily_views`, `ranked`.

### Template
```sql
WITH step1 AS (            -- e.g. filter events to the time window
    SELECT ...
    FROM events
    WHERE ...
),
step2 AS (                 -- e.g. one row per user
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM step1
    GROUP BY user_id
),
step3 AS (                 -- e.g. attach attributes or rank
    SELECT s.*, u.country
    FROM step2 AS s
    JOIN users AS u USING (user_id)
)
SELECT *
FROM step3
ORDER BY n DESC;
```
Comma between CTEs, only one `WITH`, and no comma before the final `SELECT`.

### Worked example 1: a CTE used twice
**Question:** "Users whose total watch time is above the average user's total watch time." (Average over viewers.)

```sql
WITH per_user AS (
    SELECT user_id, SUM(watch_sec) AS total_watch
    FROM views
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT p.user_id, u.username, p.total_watch
FROM per_user AS p
JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = p.user_id
WHERE p.total_watch > (SELECT AVG(total_watch) FROM per_user)
ORDER BY p.total_watch DESC;
```

Result:

| user_id | username | total_watch |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | ben | 159 |

The average of the five totals is 325 / 5 = 65, so only `ben` (159) qualifies; `ana` (64) is just below. Compare with the derived-table version in [Subqueries](#sql-subqueries): the per-user step is written once.

### Worked example 2: a pipeline of steps
**Question:** "For each creator: total watch time on their videos, their share of all watch time, and the country of the creator. Include creators with no views."

```sql
WITH video_watch AS (                       -- one row per video
    SELECT video_id, COALESCE(SUM(watch_sec), 0) AS watch
    FROM views
    GROUP BY video_id
),
creator_watch AS (                          -- one row per creator (all creators)
    SELECT vd.creator_id, COALESCE(SUM(vw.watch), 0) AS watch
    FROM videos AS vd
    LEFT JOIN video_watch AS vw ON vw.video_id = vd.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.creator_id
),
total AS (
    SELECT SUM(watch) AS all_watch FROM creator_watch
)
SELECT c.creator_id, u.username, u.country, c.watch,
       ROUND(100.0 * c.watch / t.all_watch, 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM creator_watch AS c
JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = c.creator_id
CROSS JOIN total AS t
ORDER BY c.watch DESC;
```

Result:

| creator_id | username | country | watch | pct_of_total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | ben | US | 140 | 43.1 |
| 1 | ana | KR | 136 | 41.8 |
| 3 | chen | CN | 49 | 15.1 |
| 4 | dana | US | 0 | 0.0 |

Step by step: views to video grain, videos to creator grain (LEFT JOIN keeps creator 4 with 0), a one-row total, and a `CROSS JOIN` to bring the total next to every row. The shares add up to 100. The same share can be computed with a window function: `100.0 * watch / SUM(watch) OVER ()` (see [Window functions](#sql-window-ranking)).

### Worked example 3: debugging step by step
When the final number looks wrong, replace the final `SELECT` with `SELECT * FROM creator_watch` and check the grain: one row per creator, 4 rows. This is the main practical advantage of CTEs in an exam with a live database.

### Dialect notes
- Supported in PostgreSQL, SQLite, BigQuery, Snowflake, SQL Server, and MySQL 8.0 or newer (not MySQL 5.7).
- PostgreSQL 12+ inlines a CTE used once; `MATERIALIZED` / `NOT MATERIALIZED` forces the choice. Older PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs (an optimization fence). BigQuery re-evaluates a CTE each time it is referenced.
- `WITH RECURSIVE` (PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL; BigQuery uses `WITH RECURSIVE` too) is for hierarchies and sequences, see [Recursive CTEs](#sql-recursive-cte).
- SQL Server needs a semicolon before `WITH` if the previous statement did not end with one.

### Exam angle
- Say your plan as CTE names before writing: "I will write `per_user`, then `ranked`, then filter." Examiners often give credit for a correct plan even if a detail is wrong.
- Follow-ups: "Is a CTE faster than a subquery?" Model answer: "Usually it is the same plan; the optimizer inlines it. The benefit is readability and reuse. On some engines a CTE referenced several times is computed several times, so for a heavy step used often I would create a temporary table."
- Many big-tech SQL answers are 3 to 5 CTEs long. That is normal.

### Traps
- A comma after the last CTE, or a second `WITH` keyword.
- Mixing grains inside one CTE (per user and per view columns together).
- Using `ORDER BY` inside a CTE and expecting the final output to be ordered. Only the final `ORDER BY` counts.
- Forgetting that a CTE is not a table: it does not exist in the next statement.
- Name collisions: a CTE named like a real table hides the table.

### Complexity
Same as the equivalent subqueries. The cost comes from the steps (joins, `COUNT(DISTINCT)`, sorts), not from using `WITH`.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 8, reviewed on days 9 and 14, and used in almost every question from day 12 on.
- Related: [Subqueries](#sql-subqueries), [Recursive CTEs](#sql-recursive-cte), [Retention](#sql-retention), [Funnels](#sql-funnels), [Joins: aggregate before joining](#sql-joins). pandas: each CTE becomes a named DataFrame (`per_user = views.groupby(...)`), see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents).
- External: [PostgreSQL WITH queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html), [SQLite WITH clause](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html), [LeetCode 1341 Movie Rating](https://leetcode.com/problems/movie-rating/), [LeetCode 1321 Restaurant Growth](https://leetcode.com/problems/restaurant-growth/).

sections.title: Dates and times
sections.summary: Truncate, extract, add and subtract dates in each dialect; use half-open ranges and know the time zone.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "daily", "weekly", "monthly", "per day", "in the last 7 days", "within N days of signup", "weekday", "hour of day", "first", "since". Almost every product question at TikTok or Google has a time dimension, and date syntax is the part that differs most between dialects. Tell the examiner which dialect you write; they rarely mind which one.

### Core idea
Four operations cover nearly everything: **truncate** a timestamp to a day, week or month (to group by it), **extract** a part (hour, weekday), **add** an interval (a window end), and **subtract** two dates (days between). Filter time windows with half-open ranges, `ts >= start AND ts < end`, which work for both dates and timestamps and never double count a boundary. Know the time zone of the data: "daily active users" in UTC and in Korea time are different numbers.

### Dialect table
| Task | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite | BigQuery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Today | `CURRENT_DATE` | `CURDATE()` | `date('now')` | `CURRENT_DATE()` |
| Timestamp to date | `ts::date` or `CAST(ts AS DATE)` | `DATE(ts)` | `date(ts)` | `DATE(ts)` |
| Start of month | `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)` | `DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m-01')` | `date(ts, 'start of month')` | `DATE_TRUNC(d, MONTH)`, `TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(ts, MONTH)` |
| Start of week | `DATE_TRUNC('week', ts)` (Monday) | `DATE_SUB(DATE(ts), INTERVAL WEEKDAY(ts) DAY)` | `date(ts, 'weekday 0', '-6 days')` (Monday) | `DATE_TRUNC(d, WEEK(MONDAY))` |
| Hour | `EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ts)` | `HOUR(ts)` | `CAST(strftime('%H', ts) AS INTEGER)` | `EXTRACT(HOUR FROM ts)` |
| Day of week | `EXTRACT(DOW FROM ts)` 0 = Sunday | `DAYOFWEEK(ts)` 1 = Sunday | `strftime('%w', ts)` 0 = Sunday (text) | `EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM ts)` 1 = Sunday |
| Add 7 days | `d + INTERVAL '7 days'` | `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY)` | `date(d, '+7 days')` | `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY)` |
| Days between | `d2 - d1` (dates give an integer) | `DATEDIFF(d2, d1)` | `julianday(d2) - julianday(d1)` | `DATE_DIFF(d2, d1, DAY)` |
| Date literal | `DATE '2024-03-01'` | `'2024-03-01'` | `'2024-03-01'` (text) | `DATE '2024-03-01'` |
| Format as text | `TO_CHAR(ts, 'YYYY-MM')` | `DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m')` | `strftime('%Y-%m', ts)` | `FORMAT_DATE('%Y-%m', d)` |

SQL Server: `CAST(ts AS DATE)`, `DATEADD(day, 7, d)`, `DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2)` (note the argument order), `DATETRUNC(month, ts)` from SQL Server 2022. Snowflake: `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)`, `DATEADD(day, 7, d)`, `DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2)`.

### Template
```sql
-- daily metric over a half-open window (PostgreSQL style)
SELECT CAST(view_ts AS DATE)        AS day,
       COUNT(*)                     AS n_views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)      AS dau
FROM views
WHERE view_ts >= DATE '2024-03-01'
  AND view_ts <  DATE '2024-03-01' + INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

### Worked example 1: daily views and daily active users (SQLite)
```sql
SELECT date(view_ts)            AS day,
       COUNT(*)                 AS n_views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)  AS dau
FROM views
WHERE view_ts >= '2024-03-01' AND view_ts < '2024-03-08'
GROUP BY date(view_ts)
ORDER BY day;
```

Result:

| day | n_views | dau |
|---|---|---|
| 2024-03-01 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-03-02 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-03-03 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-03-04 | 1 | 1 |
| 2024-03-05 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-03-06 | 2 | 2 |
| 2024-03-07 | 2 | 2 |

Every day here has views. In real data some days are empty and simply do not appear; to show them with 0, LEFT JOIN from a calendar table (generated with `generate_series` in PostgreSQL, `GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY` in BigQuery, or a [recursive CTE](#sql-recursive-cte)).

### Worked example 2: days from signup to first view
**Question:** "For each user, how many days after signup did they first watch a video?"

```sql
WITH first_view AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(view_ts) AS first_ts
    FROM views
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.username, u.signup_date, date(f.first_ts) AS first_view_day,
       CAST(julianday(date(f.first_ts)) - julianday(u.signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_to_first_view
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN first_view AS f ON f.user_id = u.user_id
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| username | signup_date | first_view_day | days_to_first_view |
|---|---|---|---|
| ana | 2024-01-03 | 2024-03-02 | 59 |
| ben | 2024-01-10 | 2024-03-01 | 51 |
| chen | 2024-02-01 | 2024-03-01 | 29 |
| dana | 2024-02-15 | 2024-03-02 | 16 |
| eli | 2024-03-01 | 2024-03-04 | 3 |
| fay | 2024-03-05 | NULL | NULL |

`date(...)` first removes the time of day, so the difference counts calendar days. `fay` has no view, so the result is NULL, which is honest: do not replace it with 0. PostgreSQL: `f.first_ts::date - u.signup_date`. BigQuery: `DATE_DIFF(DATE(f.first_ts), u.signup_date, DAY)`. MySQL: `DATEDIFF(f.first_ts, u.signup_date)`.

### Worked example 3: grouping by month and by weekday
```sql
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', signup_date) AS signup_month,
       COUNT(*)                       AS new_users
FROM users
GROUP BY signup_month
ORDER BY signup_month;
```

Result:

| signup_month | new_users |
|---|---|
| 2024-01 | 2 |
| 2024-02 | 2 |
| 2024-03 | 2 |

```sql
SELECT CASE strftime('%w', view_ts)
         WHEN '0' THEN 'Sun' WHEN '1' THEN 'Mon' WHEN '2' THEN 'Tue' WHEN '3' THEN 'Wed'
         WHEN '4' THEN 'Thu' WHEN '5' THEN 'Fri' ELSE 'Sat' END AS weekday,
       COUNT(*) AS n_views
FROM views
GROUP BY strftime('%w', view_ts)
ORDER BY strftime('%w', view_ts);
```

Result:

| weekday | n_views |
|---|---|
| Sun | 2 |
| Mon | 1 |
| Tue | 2 |
| Wed | 2 |
| Thu | 2 |
| Fri | 2 |
| Sat | 2 |

March 1, 2024 was a Friday. In SQLite `strftime('%w', ...)` returns text, so compare with `'0'`, not `0`.

### Worked example 4: a relative window ("last 3 days")
**Question:** "Views in the last 3 days, where today is 2024-03-07 (inclusive)."

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS views_last_3_days
FROM views
WHERE view_ts >= date('2024-03-07', '-2 days')
  AND view_ts <  date('2024-03-07', '+1 day');
```

Result:

| views_last_3_days |
|---|
| 6 |

March 5, 6 and 7: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 views. In production replace `'2024-03-07'` with `date('now')`, `CURRENT_DATE` and so on. With `BETWEEN '2024-03-05' AND '2024-03-07'` you would lose the two views on March 7, because `'2024-03-07 13:00:00'` is greater than `'2024-03-07'`.

### Exam angle
- Typical tasks: DAU/WAU/MAU, "users active on 3 consecutive days" ([Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands)), day-1 and day-7 retention ([Retention](#sql-retention)), week-over-week change ([LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead)), 7-day rolling average ([Running totals](#sql-running-totals)).
- Follow-ups: "Which time zone?", "What is a week, Monday or Sunday start?", "What about a user who signs up at 23:59?". Model sentence: "I convert timestamps to the user's local date with `AT TIME ZONE` before truncating, because a day boundary in UTC splits Korean evening sessions."
- In BigQuery, filtering on the partition column (usually the event date) is also how you control cost.

### Traps
- `BETWEEN` with timestamps (loses the last day). Use half-open ranges.
- Wrapping the column in a function in `WHERE` (`WHERE DATE(view_ts) = '2024-03-01'`) can stop the engine from using an index or partition pruning. Prefer a range on the raw column.
- `DATEDIFF` argument order differs: MySQL `(end, start)`, SQL Server and Snowflake `(unit, start, end)`, BigQuery `(end, start, unit)`.
- Day of week numbering differs (0 or 1 for Sunday).
- Text dates sort correctly only in ISO format `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- Mixing dates and timestamps: `ts = '2024-03-01'` matches only midnight.

### Complexity
Date functions are cheap, `O(1)` per row. The real cost is scanning: a filter on a partitioned date column reads only those partitions.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 9, reviewed on days 10, 13, 14 and 16 (retention).
- Related: [LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead), [Running totals and rolling windows](#sql-running-totals), [Retention](#sql-retention), [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands). pandas: `pd.to_datetime`, `.dt.floor('D')`, `.dt.to_period('M')`, `.dt.dayofweek` (0 = Monday), `resample`, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- External: [PostgreSQL date/time functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-datetime.html), [SQLite date and time functions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html), [BigQuery date functions](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/date_functions), [LeetCode 197 Rising Temperature](https://leetcode.com/problems/rising-temperature/), [LeetCode 1141 User Activity for the Past 30 Days I](https://leetcode.com/problems/user-activity-for-the-past-30-days-i/).

sections.title: Window functions: ranking and group values on every row
sections.summary: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK and aggregates OVER (PARTITION BY ...): compute per-group values without collapsing rows.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "rank", "top", "first", "latest", "for each X, the ... ", "compared to the group average", "share of the category", "percent of total", "deduplicate keeping the newest". The key difference from `GROUP BY`: the output keeps every input row and adds a column computed over a group of related rows (the window).

### Core idea
`function() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY o)` computes the function for each row over the rows with the same `p`, in the order `o`. `PARTITION BY` is like `GROUP BY` without collapsing; `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` defines the ranking order (and, for aggregates, a running frame, see [Running totals](#sql-running-totals)). Windows are computed after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, so you can rank aggregated values, but you cannot filter on a window in the same query's `WHERE` (see [Logical query order](#sql-query-order)).

| Function | Ties | Values for scores 4, 3, 2, 2, 2, 0 | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ROW_NUMBER()` | arbitrary order, no ties | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 | exactly one row per group, dedup |
| `RANK()` | same rank, then a gap | 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 6 | "top 3 including ties", competition rank |
| `DENSE_RANK()` | same rank, no gap | 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4 | "Nth highest distinct value" |
| `NTILE(k)` | splits into k buckets of near-equal size | | quartiles, deciles |
| `PERCENT_RANK()`, `CUME_DIST()` | relative position 0 to 1 | | percentiles, see [Median and percentiles](#sql-median-percentiles) |
| `SUM/AVG/COUNT/MIN/MAX() OVER (PARTITION BY p)` | | | group total next to each row, share of total |

### Template
```sql
SELECT p, x, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY score DESC, x) AS rn,     -- tie breaker x
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY score DESC)    AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY score DESC)    AS drnk,
       SUM(score)   OVER (PARTITION BY p)                        AS group_total,
       1.0 * score / SUM(score) OVER (PARTITION BY p)            AS share
FROM t;
-- named window (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, SQLite, BigQuery):
-- ... OVER w ... WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY score DESC)
```

### Worked example 1: the three ranking functions on ties
**Question:** "Rank all videos by number of views." (Video 15 has 0 views, so start from `videos`.)

```sql
WITH video_views AS (
    SELECT vd.video_id, COUNT(v.view_id) AS n_views
    FROM videos AS vd
    LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.video_id = vd.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.video_id
)
SELECT video_id, n_views,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY n_views DESC, video_id) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY n_views DESC)           AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY n_views DESC)           AS dense_rnk
FROM video_views
ORDER BY n_views DESC, video_id;
```

Result:

| video_id | n_views | row_num | rnk | dense_rnk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 12 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| 11 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 13 | 2 | 4 | 3 | 3 |
| 14 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 3 |
| 15 | 0 | 6 | 6 | 4 |

Videos 11, 13 and 14 tie with 2 views. `RANK` gives all three rank 3 and then jumps to 6; `DENSE_RANK` continues with 4. `ROW_NUMBER` needs the tie breaker `video_id` to be deterministic.

### Worked example 2: rank inside groups (PARTITION BY)
**Question:** "Within each category, rank videos by total watch time."

```sql
WITH video_watch AS (
    SELECT vd.video_id, vd.category, COALESCE(SUM(v.watch_sec), 0) AS watch
    FROM videos AS vd
    LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.video_id = vd.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.video_id, vd.category
)
SELECT category, video_id, watch,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY watch DESC) AS rank_in_category
FROM video_watch
ORDER BY category, rank_in_category;
```

Result:

| category | video_id | watch | rank_in_category |
|---|---|---|---|
| comedy | 11 | 40 | 1 |
| comedy | 15 | 0 | 2 |
| dance | 12 | 140 | 1 |
| dance | 10 | 96 | 2 |
| dance | 14 | 24 | 3 |
| food | 13 | 25 | 1 |

The ranking restarts at 1 for each category.

### Worked example 3: group values next to each row (share of total)
**Question:** "For each video: its watch time, its category's total, and its share of the category."

```sql
WITH video_watch AS (
    SELECT vd.video_id, vd.category, COALESCE(SUM(v.watch_sec), 0) AS watch
    FROM videos AS vd
    LEFT JOIN views AS v ON v.video_id = vd.video_id
    GROUP BY vd.video_id, vd.category
)
SELECT category, video_id, watch,
       SUM(watch) OVER (PARTITION BY category)                         AS category_watch,
       ROUND(100.0 * watch / SUM(watch) OVER (PARTITION BY category), 1) AS pct_of_category,
       ROUND(100.0 * watch / SUM(watch) OVER (), 1)                    AS pct_of_all
FROM video_watch
ORDER BY category, watch DESC;
```

Result:

| category | video_id | watch | category_watch | pct_of_category | pct_of_all |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| comedy | 11 | 40 | 40 | 100.0 | 12.3 |
| comedy | 15 | 0 | 40 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| dance | 12 | 140 | 260 | 53.8 | 43.1 |
| dance | 10 | 96 | 260 | 36.9 | 29.5 |
| dance | 14 | 24 | 260 | 9.2 | 7.4 |
| food | 13 | 25 | 25 | 100.0 | 7.7 |

`OVER ()` with nothing inside is the whole result. This replaces the self-join or the scalar subquery you would otherwise need.

### Window vs GROUP BY
| | `GROUP BY` | Window function |
|---|---|---|
| Output rows | one per group | one per input row |
| Can show row details next to group value | no (needs a join back) | yes |
| Filter on result | `HAVING` | outer query or `QUALIFY` |
| Typical question | "total per category" | "rank within category", "share of category" |

### Exam angle
- The most asked SQL topic after joins at big tech. Expect: "difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK", "rank users by watch time within each country", "dedup keeping the latest row".
- Model answer for RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER: "All three number rows in the window order. ROW_NUMBER never ties, so I use it when I need exactly one row per group. RANK gives ties the same number and leaves gaps; DENSE_RANK leaves no gaps, so DENSE_RANK = 2 is the second highest distinct value."
- Follow-up: "What happens with ties if you use ROW_NUMBER?" One tied row is dropped arbitrarily unless you add a tie breaker; say which tie breaker the business wants (newest, smallest id).

### Traps
- Filtering on a window in the same `WHERE` (not allowed). Wrap in a CTE, or use `QUALIFY` where supported.
- `ROW_NUMBER` without a unique tie breaker gives non-deterministic results that can change between runs.
- Forgetting `PARTITION BY`: the ranking runs over the whole table.
- Integer division in shares: `watch / SUM(watch) OVER ()` is 0 in PostgreSQL and SQLite with integer inputs.
- NULLs in the `ORDER BY` of the window sort first or last depending on the dialect (see [SQL basics](#sql-basics)). Use `NULLS LAST` where supported or `COALESCE`.
- An `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` with an aggregate (`SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY t)`) gives a running total, not the group total. That is a frame topic: [Running totals](#sql-running-totals).

### Complexity
One sort per partition order: `O(n log n)`. Several windows with the same `PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY` share one sort. Much cheaper than a correlated subquery, which is `O(n x m)` in the worst case.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 10, reviewed on days 11 and 14; used again in [Top N](#sql-top-n) (day 11), [LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead) (day 12), [Running totals](#sql-running-totals) (day 13) and [Dedup](#sql-dedup-cleaning) (day 20).
- Related: [Subqueries vs windows](#sql-subqueries), [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation). pandas: `groupby().rank(method='first'|'min'|'dense')` and `groupby().transform('sum')`, see [SQL to pandas](#sql-pandas-equivalents) and [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas). Frames are the SQL version of a [sliding window](#algo-sliding-window).
- External: [PostgreSQL window function tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-window.html), [SQLite window functions](https://www.sqlite.org/windowfunctions.html), [LeetCode 178 Rank Scores](https://leetcode.com/problems/rank-scores/), [LeetCode 1077 Project Employees III](https://leetcode.com/problems/project-employees-iii/).

sections.title: Top N, top N per group, and Nth highest
sections.summary: Global top N with LIMIT, top N per group with a ranking window (or QUALIFY), and the Nth highest value with ties handled.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals: "top 3", "most", "best", "highest", "the latest per", "the first per", "second highest", "Nth". First decide two things and say them out loud: is it top N **overall** or top N **per group**, and how should **ties** be handled (keep all tied rows, or exactly N rows)?

### Core idea
| Question | Tool | Ties |
|---|---|---|
| Top N overall | `ORDER BY ... LIMIT N` | cuts ties arbitrarily |
| Top N overall, keep ties | `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ...) <= N` | keeps all tied rows |
| Top N per group | `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY ...) <= N` in an outer query | exactly N per group |
| Top N per group, keep ties | `RANK()` or `DENSE_RANK()` instead of `ROW_NUMBER()` | may return more than N |
| Nth highest distinct value | `DENSE_RANK() = N`, or `LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1` on `DISTINCT` values | counts equal values once |
| Must return NULL if it does not exist | wrap in a scalar subquery | |

`LIMIT` works only for the whole result, never per group. Per group always means a window function (or a correlated subquery).

### Template
```sql
-- top N per group (works everywhere with window functions)
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT g, item, score,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY score DESC, item) AS rn
    FROM t
)
SELECT g, item, score FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

-- BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, DuckDB, Teradata: QUALIFY filters on the window directly
SELECT g, item, score
FROM t
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY score DESC, item) <= 3;
```

| Dialect | Top 3 overall |
|---|---|
