```sql
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | sessions | events | events_per_session |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 11 | 1.38 |
| 2 | 11 | 14 | 1.27 |
| 3 | 6 | 7 | 1.17 |
| 4 | 5 | 6 | 1.2 |
| 5 | 1 | 3 | 3.0 |


### Worked example 3: find the gaps (missing days)
Question: "For user 1, list each period of inactivity between two active days: the first and last missing day."

```sql
WITH active AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(event_ts) AS day FROM events
),
nxt AS (
  SELECT user_id, day,
         LEAD(day) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) AS next_day
  FROM active
)
SELECT user_id,
       DATE(day, '+1 day')       AS gap_start,
       DATE(next_day, '-1 day')  AS gap_end,
       CAST(julianday(next_day) - julianday(day) - 1 AS INTEGER) AS missing_days
FROM nxt
WHERE user_id = 1
  AND julianday(next_day) - julianday(day) > 1
ORDER BY day;
```

Result:

| user_id | gap_start | gap_end | missing_days |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2024-01-08 | 2024-01-09 | 2 |
| 1 | 2024-01-11 | 2024-01-19 | 9 |
| 1 | 2024-01-21 | 2024-03-01 | 41 |
| 1 | 2024-03-03 | 2024-03-05 | 3 |


A gap is where the next active day is more than 1 day later. The same logic finds missing ids (LeetCode "Find the Missing IDs" uses a [recursive CTE](#sql-recursive-cte) to list every id, then `NOT IN`).

### Exam angle
- Typical asks: longest login streak (Meta, TikTok), users active 3 or more consecutive days, "Human Traffic of Stadium" (3 or more consecutive ids with at least 100 people), sessionize a click log (also asked as a Python coding task, see [Data processing](#algo-data-processing)), start and end of continuous ranges.
- Follow-ups: "Streak that is still active today?" (filter islands whose `end_day` = the last date). "What if a user can skip one day without breaking the streak?" (use the flag method with `gap > 2`). "Do it in pandas?" (`(s.diff() != 1).cumsum()` gives the island id; see [pandas equivalents](#sql-pandas-equivalents)).
- A strong answer sounds like: "I deduplicate to one row per user per day, subtract the row number from the date so each consecutive run gets a constant key, group by that key and take the count. For sessions I flag rows where the gap to the previous event exceeds 30 minutes and take a running sum of the flag."

### Traps
- Not deduplicating days before `ROW_NUMBER()`.
- Using `RANK()` or `DENSE_RANK()` instead of `ROW_NUMBER()` in the difference trick.
- Subtracting a number from a text date in SQLite (`'2024-01-03' - 1` gives 2023, a number). Use `julianday(day)`.
- Forgetting `PARTITION BY user_id`, so streaks continue across users.
- Using the default `RANGE` frame for the running sum of flags when timestamps tie (see [Running totals](#sql-running-totals)).
- Off-by-one in gap boundaries: the gap starts the day after an active day and ends the day before the next one.

### Complexity
One sort per user for `ROW_NUMBER()` or `LAG()` (`O(n log n)`), then a linear `GROUP BY`. The flag method needs two windows that share the same order, so it is still one sort.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 19 (focus), reviewed on days 20, 21 and 24.
- Related: [LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead), [Running totals](#sql-running-totals), [Window ranking](#sql-window-ranking), [Recursive CTE](#sql-recursive-cte), [Sorting and intervals](#algo-sorting-intervals), [Data processing](#algo-data-processing).
- LeetCode: [Human Traffic of Stadium](https://leetcode.com/problems/human-traffic-of-stadium/), [Find the Start and End Number of Continuous Ranges](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-start-and-end-number-of-continuous-ranges/), [Consecutive Numbers](https://leetcode.com/problems/consecutive-numbers/).
- Docs: [SQLite window functions](https://www.sqlite.org/windowfunctions.html), [SQLite date and time functions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html).

sections.title: Deduplication and data cleaning
sections.summary: Use when the data has duplicate rows, several versions per key, messy strings or NULLs to fix before you aggregate.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals in the question:
- "the table may contain duplicate rows", "events can be logged twice", "client retries"
- "keep the latest record per user", "current status", "most recent address"
- "find duplicate emails", "delete duplicates but keep the smallest id"
- messy values: `' View'`, `'VIEW'`, empty strings, NULLs, numbers stored as text

What it is NOT: top-N per group with N > 1 is [Top N](#sql-top-n), although the tool (`ROW_NUMBER`) is the same.

### Core idea
First define what "the same record" means: the dedup key (for example `user_id, video_id, event_type, event_ts`). Then clean the key columns so equal things look equal (`LOWER(TRIM(event_type))`). Then keep one row per key: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY preference) AS rn` and filter `rn = 1`. The `ORDER BY` says which copy wins (latest `updated_at`, non-NULL value first, smallest id). `DISTINCT` only works when whole rows are identical; `ROW_NUMBER` works when rows differ in columns outside the key. Tiny example: rows (user 1, android, Nov) and (user 1, ios, Jan) with `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` keep (user 1, ios, Jan).

This section uses two small made-up tables: `events_raw` (same columns as `events`, with duplicates and messy strings) and `user_devices(user_id, device, updated_at)` (device history).

```sql
SELECT * FROM events_raw;
```

Result:

| user_id | video_id | event_type | event_ts | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | view | 2024-01-05 09:00:00 | 25 |
| 1 | 10 | view | 2024-01-05 09:00:00 | 25 |
| 1 | 10 |  Like | 2024-01-05 09:01:00 | NULL |
| 2 | 10 | VIEW | 2024-01-10 12:00:00 | 30 |
| 2 | 10 | view | 2024-01-10 12:00:00 | 30 |
| 2 | 10 | like | 2024-01-10 12:10:00 | NULL |
| 3 | 10 | view | 2024-02-01 10:00:00 | NULL |
| 3 | 10 | view | 2024-02-01 10:00:05 | 30 |


### Template
```sql
-- generic template: keep one row per key
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key_col_1, key_col_2
                            ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM t
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
```

### Worked example 1: find the duplicates first
Question: "Which events appear more than once?" Always look before you delete.

```sql
SELECT user_id, video_id, LOWER(TRIM(event_type)) AS event_type, event_ts,
       COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM events_raw
GROUP BY user_id, video_id, LOWER(TRIM(event_type)), event_ts
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | video_id | event_type | event_ts | copies |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | view | 2024-01-05 09:00:00 | 2 |
| 2 | 10 | view | 2024-01-10 12:00:00 | 2 |


Without `LOWER(TRIM(...))` only user 1's row is a duplicate. `'VIEW'` and `'view'` are different strings until you normalize them. This is LeetCode "Duplicate Emails" (`GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`).

### Worked example 2: clean and deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER
Question: "Build a clean events table: normalized event types and one row per (user, video, event type, timestamp)."

```sql
WITH cleaned AS (
  SELECT user_id, video_id, LOWER(TRIM(event_type)) AS event_type, event_ts, watch_sec
  FROM events_raw
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, video_id, event_type, event_ts
                            ORDER BY watch_sec DESC) AS rn
  FROM cleaned
)
SELECT user_id, video_id, event_type, event_ts, watch_sec
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts;
```

Result:

| user_id | video_id | event_type | event_ts | watch_sec |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | view | 2024-01-05 09:00:00 | 25 |
| 1 | 10 | like | 2024-01-05 09:01:00 | NULL |
| 2 | 10 | view | 2024-01-10 12:00:00 | 30 |
| 2 | 10 | like | 2024-01-10 12:10:00 | NULL |
| 3 | 10 | view | 2024-02-01 10:00:00 | NULL |
| 3 | 10 | view | 2024-02-01 10:00:05 | 30 |


8 raw rows became 6. Clean first, then rank, because the key must use the cleaned values. User 3 still has two views 5 seconds apart: they have different timestamps, so the exact key keeps both. Example 4 handles that.

### Worked example 3: latest record per key, and the tie trap
Question: "Give each user's current device (the row with the latest `updated_at`)."

```sql
SELECT * FROM user_devices ORDER BY user_id, updated_at;
```

Result:

| user_id | device | updated_at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | android | 2023-11-02 |
| 1 | ios | 2024-01-03 |
| 2 | android | 2024-01-10 |
| 3 | ios | 2024-02-01 |
| 3 | web | 2024-02-20 |
| 3 | android | 2024-02-20 |


A common first answer joins to the maximum date:

```sql
SELECT d.user_id, d.device, d.updated_at
FROM user_devices AS d
JOIN (SELECT user_id, MAX(updated_at) AS max_at
      FROM user_devices GROUP BY user_id) AS m
  ON m.user_id = d.user_id AND m.max_at = d.updated_at
ORDER BY d.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | device | updated_at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ios | 2024-01-03 |
| 2 | android | 2024-01-10 |
| 3 | web | 2024-02-20 |
| 3 | android | 2024-02-20 |


User 3 appears twice, because two rows share the latest date. `ROW_NUMBER` always returns exactly one row per user:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT user_id, device, updated_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, device) AS rn
  FROM user_devices
)
SELECT user_id, device, updated_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | device | updated_at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ios | 2024-01-03 |
| 2 | android | 2024-01-10 |
| 3 | android | 2024-02-20 |


Add a tie breaker (`device` here, an id or ingestion time in real data) so the result is deterministic. If the question wants all tied rows, use `RANK()` instead (see [Window ranking](#sql-window-ranking)).

### Worked example 4: near duplicates (retries a few seconds apart)
Question: "Treat events with the same user, video and type that happen within 10 seconds of the previous one as one event. Keep the first timestamp and the largest `watch_sec`."

```sql
WITH cleaned AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, video_id, LOWER(TRIM(event_type)) AS event_type, event_ts, watch_sec
  FROM events_raw
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT *,
         CASE WHEN LAG(event_ts) OVER w IS NULL
                OR (julianday(event_ts) - julianday(LAG(event_ts) OVER w)) * 86400 > 10
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_burst
  FROM cleaned
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id, video_id, event_type ORDER BY event_ts)
),
bursts AS (
  SELECT *,
         SUM(new_burst) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, video_id, event_type ORDER BY event_ts
                              ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS burst_id
  FROM flagged
)
SELECT user_id, video_id, event_type,
       MIN(event_ts) AS event_ts, MAX(watch_sec) AS watch_sec, COUNT(*) AS raw_rows
FROM bursts
GROUP BY user_id, video_id, event_type, burst_id
ORDER BY user_id, event_ts;
```

Result:

| user_id | video_id | event_type | event_ts | watch_sec | raw_rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | view | 2024-01-05 09:00:00 | 25 | 1 |
| 1 | 10 | like | 2024-01-05 09:01:00 | NULL | 1 |
| 2 | 10 | view | 2024-01-10 12:00:00 | 30 | 1 |
| 2 | 10 | like | 2024-01-10 12:10:00 | NULL | 1 |
| 3 | 10 | view | 2024-02-01 10:00:00 | 30 | 2 |


This is the flag and running sum trick from [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands). The `WINDOW w AS (...)` clause names a window once and reuses it (SQLite 3.28+, PostgreSQL and MySQL 8). User 3's two rows became one row with the first timestamp and the non-NULL watch time. `MAX` ignores NULLs, which is what we want here.

### Worked example 5: delete duplicates in place
Question (LeetCode "Delete Duplicate Emails"): "Delete duplicate rows but keep one copy." SQLite has a hidden `rowid` you can use as the id.

```sql
DELETE FROM events_raw
WHERE rowid NOT IN (
  SELECT MIN(rowid)
  FROM events_raw
  GROUP BY user_id, video_id, LOWER(TRIM(event_type)), event_ts
);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_left FROM events_raw;
```

Result:

| rows_left |
|---|
| 6 |


In PostgreSQL use the primary key (or `ctid`) the same way. In MySQL you cannot select from the table you delete from in a plain subquery, so the usual answer is a self join: `DELETE p1 FROM person p1 JOIN person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id`. In an analytics exam, prefer building a clean table or view over deleting raw data.

### Cleaning functions you will need
| Problem | SQL | Note |
|---|---|---|
| spaces and case | `LOWER(TRIM(col))` | `UPPER`, `LTRIM`, `RTRIM` also exist |
| empty string should be NULL | `NULLIF(TRIM(col), '')` | |
| NULL should be a default | `COALESCE(col, 0)` | first non-NULL argument |
| number stored as text | `CAST(col AS REAL)` | PostgreSQL also `col::numeric` |
| remove characters | `REPLACE(col, ',', '')` | for `'10,000+'` style values also remove `'+'` |
| part of a string | `SUBSTR(col, 1, 7)` | `'2024-01-15'` gives `'2024-01'` |
| invalid category | `CASE WHEN col IN ('view', 'like', 'share', 'comment') THEN col END` | everything else becomes NULL |
| date from timestamp | `DATE(ts)` | PostgreSQL `ts::date`, MySQL `DATE(ts)` |

### Exam angle
- Typical asks: "Events may be logged twice; count unique views", "latest status per order", "second most recent purchase", "remove test accounts and bots before computing the metric".
- Follow-ups: "How do you know there are duplicates?" (compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(DISTINCT key)`). "Which copy do you keep and why?" "How would you stop this upstream?" (idempotent event ids, unique constraints).
- A strong answer sounds like: "I first check `COUNT(*)` against `COUNT(DISTINCT key)`. Then I normalize the key columns and keep one row per key with ROW_NUMBER, ordering by updated_at descending with a tie breaker, because a join to MAX(updated_at) returns several rows on ties."

### Traps
- `DISTINCT` on all columns does not remove rows that differ in one column (for example a NULL versus a value).
- Joining to `MAX(date)` returns duplicates when there are ties.
- Ranking on raw values when the key should use cleaned values.
- `ROW_NUMBER` without a tie breaker gives a random winner, so results change between runs.
- `NULL = NULL` is not true: rows with NULL in a key column do not match in a join, but `GROUP BY` and `PARTITION BY` do put NULLs together.
- Deleting data in an analytics answer when a filtered view is enough.

### Complexity
`GROUP BY` or `ROW_NUMBER` over the key: one hash or sort pass, `O(n)` to `O(n log n)`. The `NOT IN (SELECT MIN(rowid) ...)` delete is fine on small tables; on large tables use a join or build a new table.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 20 (focus), reviewed on days 21 and 27.
- Related: [Window ranking](#sql-window-ranking), [Top N per group](#sql-top-n), [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands), [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls), [pandas drop_duplicates](#sql-pandas-equivalents), [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- LeetCode: [Duplicate Emails](https://leetcode.com/problems/duplicate-emails/), [Delete Duplicate Emails](https://leetcode.com/problems/delete-duplicate-emails/), [Fix Names in a Table](https://leetcode.com/problems/fix-names-in-a-table/).
- Docs: [SQLite core functions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_corefunc.html).

sections.title: Pivot and unpivot (CASE WHEN aggregation)
sections.summary: Use when the answer needs one row per entity and one column per category, or the reverse.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals in the question:
- "one row per user with columns for views, likes and shares"
- "show January, February and March as columns", "a column per country"
- "a cohort table with month 0, month 1, month 2 as columns"
- the reverse: "turn these columns into rows" (unpivot), for example LeetCode "Rearrange Products Table"

What it is NOT: if the output should stay one row per (entity, category), that is a normal `GROUP BY entity, category` ([Aggregation](#sql-aggregation)). Pivot only changes the shape for reading.

### Core idea
Standard SQL has no portable `PIVOT`, so you write one conditional aggregate per output column: `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'x' THEN value ELSE 0 END) AS x`. Group by the row key. Every row of the group passes through every `CASE`, and each `CASE` keeps only its own category. Use `COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END)` or `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` for counts, and `MAX(CASE WHEN ... THEN value END)` when there is exactly one value per cell (for example a retention percent). The column list must be written by hand, because SQL needs to know the output columns before it runs. Unpivot is the reverse: one `SELECT` per column, glued with `UNION ALL`. Tiny example: long rows (ana, view), (ana, view), (ana, like) become one wide row (ana, views = 2, likes = 1).

### Template
```sql
-- generic template
SELECT row_key,
       SUM(CASE WHEN col_key = 'a' THEN value ELSE 0 END) AS a,
       SUM(CASE WHEN col_key = 'b' THEN value ELSE 0 END) AS b,
       SUM(value) AS total
FROM long_table
GROUP BY row_key;
```

### Worked example 1: one row per user, one column per event type
Question: "For every user, including users with no activity, show the number of views, likes, shares and comments."

```sql
SELECT u.user_id, u.username,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'view'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS views,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'like'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS likes,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'share'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shares,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type = 'comment' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS comments,
       COUNT(e.event_type) AS all_events
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN events AS e ON e.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username
ORDER BY u.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | username | views | likes | shares | comments | all_events |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | 9 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 11 |
| 2 | ben | 11 | 2 | 0 | 1 | 14 |
| 3 | chen | 6 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 7 |
| 4 | dana | 5 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 6 |
| 5 | eli | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 3 |
| 6 | fay | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |


Fay has one joined row with NULLs from the LEFT JOIN. Every `CASE` gives 0 for it, and `COUNT(e.event_type)` gives 0 because it skips NULL (`COUNT(*)` would wrongly give 1). If you wrote `ELSE NULL` (or no `ELSE`), fay's columns would be NULL instead of 0; wrap them in `COALESCE(..., 0)` in that case.

### Worked example 2: categories as rows, months as columns
Question: "Total watch seconds per category, with one column per month of 2024."

```sql
SELECT v.category,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', e.event_ts) = '01' THEN e.watch_sec ELSE 0 END) AS jan,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', e.event_ts) = '02' THEN e.watch_sec ELSE 0 END) AS feb,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', e.event_ts) = '03' THEN e.watch_sec ELSE 0 END) AS mar,
       SUM(e.watch_sec) AS total
FROM events AS e
JOIN videos AS v ON v.video_id = e.video_id
WHERE e.event_type = 'view'
GROUP BY v.category
ORDER BY total DESC;
```

Result:

| category | jan | feb | mar | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dance | 278 | 170 | 260 | 708 |
| comedy | 45 | 45 | 40 | 130 |
| food | 0 | 38 | 25 | 63 |


Look at comedy in March: chen's view has NULL `watch_sec`. `CASE` returns NULL for that row and `SUM` skips it, so the total is still correct. A video that was uploaded but never watched (video 15, comedy) adds nothing because of the inner join; that is fine for watch time.

### Worked example 3: cohort retention table with month offsets as columns
Question: "Turn the cohort retention list from [Retention](#sql-retention) into a table with one row per signup month and columns m0, m1, m2."

```sql
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT user_id, strftime('%Y-%m', signup_date) AS cohort_month,
         CAST(strftime('%Y', signup_date) AS INTEGER) * 12
           + CAST(strftime('%m', signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS cohort_idx
  FROM users
),
monthly AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
         CAST(strftime('%Y', event_ts) AS INTEGER) * 12
           + CAST(strftime('%m', event_ts) AS INTEGER) AS month_idx
  FROM events
),
long AS (
  SELECT c.cohort_month, m.month_idx - c.cohort_idx AS k, COUNT(*) AS active
  FROM cohort AS c
  JOIN monthly AS m ON m.user_id = c.user_id
  GROUP BY c.cohort_month, k
),
sizes AS (
  SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS n FROM cohort GROUP BY cohort_month
)
SELECT s.cohort_month, s.n AS cohort_size,
       ROUND(100.0 * MAX(CASE WHEN l.k = 0 THEN l.active END) / s.n, 1) AS m0,
       ROUND(100.0 * MAX(CASE WHEN l.k = 1 THEN l.active END) / s.n, 1) AS m1,
       ROUND(100.0 * MAX(CASE WHEN l.k = 2 THEN l.active END) / s.n, 1) AS m2
FROM sizes AS s
LEFT JOIN long AS l ON l.cohort_month = s.cohort_month
GROUP BY s.cohort_month, s.n
ORDER BY s.cohort_month;
```

Result:

| cohort_month | cohort_size | m0 | m1 | m2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01 | 2 | 100.0 | 50.0 | 100.0 |
| 2024-02 | 2 | 100.0 | 100.0 | NULL |
| 2024-03 | 2 | 50.0 | NULL | NULL |


`MAX(CASE ... END)` without `ELSE` leaves NULL where there is no data. That is correct here: the March cohort has no month 1 yet, which is "not observed", not 0 percent. This is the same "immature cohort" point as in [Retention](#sql-retention). The empty cells give the triangle shape of every real cohort table.

### Worked example 4: unpivot with UNION ALL
Question: "The table `user_stats(user_id, views, likes, shares)` is wide. Return it long: one row per (user, metric, value), skipping zeros."

```sql
WITH user_stats AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS views,
         SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'like'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS likes,
         SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'share' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shares
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT user_id, 'views' AS metric, views AS value FROM user_stats WHERE views > 0
UNION ALL
SELECT user_id, 'likes', likes FROM user_stats WHERE likes > 0
UNION ALL
SELECT user_id, 'shares', shares FROM user_stats WHERE shares > 0
ORDER BY user_id, metric;
```

Result:

| user_id | metric | value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | likes | 1 |
| 1 | shares | 1 |
| 1 | views | 9 |
| 2 | likes | 2 |
| 2 | views | 11 |
| 3 | likes | 1 |
| 3 | views | 6 |
| 4 | shares | 1 |
| 4 | views | 5 |
| 5 | likes | 1 |
| 5 | shares | 1 |
| 5 | views | 1 |


Use `UNION ALL`, not `UNION`: `UNION` removes duplicate rows and sorts, which is slower and can silently drop rows. The column names come from the first `SELECT`.

### Dialect notes
```sql
-- PostgreSQL: FILTER is a shorter conditional aggregate
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'view') AS views,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'like') AS likes
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id;
-- SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery and Oracle also have a PIVOT operator, for example
-- BigQuery: SELECT * FROM (SELECT user_id, event_type FROM events)
--           PIVOT (COUNT(*) FOR event_type IN ('view', 'like', 'share'))
```
SQLite 3.30+ also supports `FILTER`, but the `CASE` version works everywhere, so use it in exams unless the dialect is known.

### Exam angle
- Typical asks: LeetCode "Reformat Department Table" (months as columns), weekly metrics dashboard (one column per week), cohort tables, "number of users on laptop and on mobile" as two columns (DataLemur "Laptop vs. Mobile Viewership").
- Follow-ups: "What if the categories are not known in advance?" (you need dynamic SQL, or return the long format and pivot in pandas with `pivot_table`; see [pandas equivalents](#sql-pandas-equivalents)). "0 or NULL in empty cells?" (0 for counts, NULL for not observed).
- A strong answer sounds like: "I group by the row key and write one SUM(CASE WHEN ...) per output column. I start from the users table with a LEFT JOIN so inactive users get a row of zeros."

### Traps
- `COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts every row, because 0 is not NULL. With `COUNT` leave out the `ELSE`, or use `SUM`.
- Forgetting a category: rows of that category silently vanish from the output.
- `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` when unpivoting.
- Using `MAX(CASE ...)` for something that has several rows per cell. It hides duplicates; check that the grain is one value per cell first.
- Mixing up 0 and NULL in empty cells.

### Complexity
One scan and one hash aggregate: `O(n)`. Each extra column is one more `CASE` per row, which is cheap. Unpivot with `UNION ALL` scans the source once per column.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 22 (focus), reviewed on day 23.
- Related: [CASE WHEN](#sql-case-when), [Aggregation](#sql-aggregation), [Retention](#sql-retention), [Funnels](#sql-funnels), [pandas pivot_table and melt](#sql-pandas-equivalents), [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).
- LeetCode: [Reformat Department Table](https://leetcode.com/problems/reformat-department-table/), [Rearrange Products Table](https://leetcode.com/problems/rearrange-products-table/), [Monthly Transactions I](https://leetcode.com/problems/monthly-transactions-i/).
- Docs: [PostgreSQL aggregate FILTER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES).

sections.title: Median and percentiles without a MEDIAN function
sections.summary: Use when the question asks for a median, p90, quartiles or 'top 10 percent' and the engine has no MEDIAN.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals in the question:
- "median watch time", "median per category", "typical value" for a skewed metric
- "p90 / p95 / p99 latency", "90th percentile", "quartiles", "top 10 percent of users"
- "the value below which X percent of users fall"
- a frequency table: "value and how many times it occurs, find the median" (LeetCode "Find Median Given Frequency of Numbers")

Why it matters: engagement metrics (watch time, spend, sessions) are heavy-tailed, so the mean is pulled up by a few heavy users. Examiners ask for the median to see whether you know that and can compute it without a built-in function. SQLite, MySQL and older engines have no `MEDIAN`. See [Descriptive statistics](#stats-descriptive) for when to report which.

### Core idea
Sort the values, number them `1..n` with `ROW_NUMBER()`, and get `n` with `COUNT(*) OVER ()`. The median is the average of the rows at positions `(n + 1) / 2` and `(n + 2) / 2` with integer division. For odd `n` both positions are the same middle row; for even `n` they are the two middle rows. Tiny example: values 5, 9, 12, 15 give `n = 4`, positions 2 and 3, median `(9 + 12) / 2 = 10.5`. For other percentiles, use the nearest-rank rule: the p-th percentile is the smallest value whose `CUME_DIST()` (share of rows less than or equal to it) is at least `p`. Remove NULLs first: they are not values.

| Function | What it returns for a row | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x)` | position 1..n (ties get different numbers) | median by position |
| `CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY x)` | share of rows with value less than or equal, in (0, 1] | nearest-rank percentile |
| `PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x)` | `(rank - 1) / (n - 1)`, in [0, 1] | "what percentile is this user" |
| `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY x)` | bucket 1..4 of almost equal size | quartiles, deciles, top 10 percent |
| `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)` | interpolated percentile (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server as a window) | median in one line |

The examples use the `views` table from [the exam approach](#sql-exam-approach) (13 views, one with NULL `watch_sec`), which is the same as the view events in `events`.

### Template
```sql
-- generic template: median per group
WITH s AS (
  SELECT g, x,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY g)            AS n
  FROM t
  WHERE x IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT g, AVG(x) AS median_x
FROM s
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY g;
```

### Worked example 1: median watch time
Question: "What is the median `watch_sec` per view?"

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT watch_sec,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER ()                   AS n
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT rn, n, watch_sec,
       CASE WHEN rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2) THEN 'middle' END AS used
FROM s
ORDER BY rn;
```

Result:

| rn | n | watch_sec | used |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 12 | 5 | NULL |
| 2 | 12 | 9 | NULL |
| 3 | 12 | 12 | NULL |
| 4 | 12 | 15 | NULL |
| 5 | 12 | 20 | NULL |
| 6 | 12 | 24 | middle |
| 7 | 12 | 25 | middle |
| 8 | 12 | 30 | NULL |
| 9 | 12 | 30 | NULL |
| 10 | 12 | 40 | NULL |
| 11 | 12 | 55 | NULL |
| 12 | 12 | 60 | NULL |


There are 12 non-NULL values, so the positions are `13 / 2 = 6` and `14 / 2 = 7` (integer division), and the median is `(24 + 25) / 2`:

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT watch_sec,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER ()                   AS n
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT AVG(watch_sec) AS median_watch_sec,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(watch_sec), 2) FROM views) AS mean_watch_sec
FROM s
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2);
```

Result:

| median_watch_sec | mean_watch_sec |
|---|---|
| 24.5 | 27.08 |


If you forget `WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL`, the NULL row is sorted first in SQLite and gets position 1, and `n` becomes 13, which shifts the middle. Integer division is wanted here, so do not write `(n + 1) / 2.0`. A second classic way, without window functions, uses `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`:

```sql
SELECT AVG(watch_sec) AS median_watch_sec
FROM (
  SELECT watch_sec
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY watch_sec
  LIMIT 2 - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM views WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL) % 2
  OFFSET (SELECT (COUNT(*) - 1) / 2 FROM views WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL)
);
```

Result:

| median_watch_sec |
|---|
| 24.5 |


It skips `(n - 1) / 2` rows and takes 2 rows when `n` is even, 1 row when `n` is odd. PostgreSQL and SQLite accept subqueries in `LIMIT`; MySQL does not, so there use the window version.

### Worked example 2: median per category
Question: "Median watch time per video category."

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT v.category, w.watch_sec,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY v.category ORDER BY w.watch_sec) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY v.category)                      AS n
  FROM views AS w
  JOIN videos AS v ON v.video_id = w.video_id
  WHERE w.watch_sec IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT category, MAX(n) AS n_views, AVG(watch_sec) AS median_watch_sec
FROM s
WHERE rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
```

Result:

| category | n_views | median_watch_sec |
|---|---|---|
| comedy | 1 | 40.0 |
| dance | 9 | 25.0 |
| food | 2 | 12.5 |


Dance has 9 values, so positions 5 and 5: one middle value. Food has 2 values (5 and 20), so the median is their average 12.5. Comedy has only one non-NULL view: chen's view 12 is excluded by the `IS NOT NULL` filter. `PARTITION BY category` in both windows is what makes the positions restart per group.

### Worked example 3: p90 and quartiles
Question: "What is the 90th percentile of watch time, and which quartile is each view in?"

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT watch_sec,
         CUME_DIST()    OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS cume_dist,
         PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS pct_rank,
         NTILE(4)       OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS quartile
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT watch_sec, ROUND(cume_dist, 3) AS cume_dist,
       ROUND(pct_rank, 3) AS pct_rank, quartile
FROM s
ORDER BY watch_sec;
```

Result:

| watch_sec | cume_dist | pct_rank | quartile |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.083 | 0.0 | 1 |
| 9 | 0.167 | 0.091 | 1 |
| 12 | 0.25 | 0.182 | 1 |
| 15 | 0.333 | 0.273 | 2 |
| 20 | 0.417 | 0.364 | 2 |
| 24 | 0.5 | 0.455 | 2 |
| 25 | 0.583 | 0.545 | 3 |
| 30 | 0.75 | 0.636 | 3 |
| 30 | 0.75 | 0.636 | 3 |
| 40 | 0.833 | 0.818 | 4 |
| 55 | 0.917 | 0.909 | 4 |
| 60 | 1.0 | 1.0 | 4 |


The two rows with 30 are ties, so they get the same `CUME_DIST` and `PERCENT_RANK` (but `NTILE` may still split ties into different buckets). Now the p90 by nearest rank:

```sql
WITH s AS (
  SELECT watch_sec, CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS cd
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT MIN(watch_sec) AS p90_nearest_rank
FROM s
WHERE cd >= 0.9;
```

Result:

| p90_nearest_rank |
|---|
| 55 |


`0.9 * 12 = 10.8`, so the p90 is the 11th value, 55. `PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9)` in PostgreSQL would interpolate between the 10th and 11th values and give a slightly different number (`40 + 0.9 * (55 - 40) = 53.5`, using position `1 + 0.9 * (n - 1) = 10.9`). Both are accepted; say which definition you use. For "top 10 percent of users by watch time", `NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) = 1` is the usual answer.

### Worked example 4: median from a frequency table
Question (LeetCode "Find Median Given Frequency of Numbers"): "A table has `(value, frequency)`. Find the median without expanding it."

```sql
WITH freq AS (
  SELECT watch_sec AS value, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM views
  WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY watch_sec
),
c AS (
  SELECT value, cnt,
         SUM(cnt) OVER (ORDER BY value ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cum,
         SUM(cnt) OVER () AS total
  FROM freq
)
SELECT AVG(value) AS median
FROM c
WHERE cum >= total / 2.0
  AND cum - cnt <= total / 2.0;
```

Result:

| median |
|---|
| 24.5 |


A value covers positions `cum - cnt + 1` to `cum`. The condition keeps the values whose range touches the middle (`total / 2`), which gives one value for odd totals and the two middle values (or one value covering both) for even totals. This is the [running total](#sql-running-totals) pattern used for a statistic.

### Dialect notes
```sql
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS median,
       PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY watch_sec) AS p90_discrete
FROM views;
-- BigQuery: APPROX_QUANTILES(watch_sec, 100)[OFFSET(90)]; Snowflake and Oracle: MEDIAN(watch_sec)
```
`PERCENTILE_CONT` interpolates, `PERCENTILE_DISC` returns an actual value from the data. Both ignore NULLs.

### Exam angle
- Typical asks: median time between signup and first purchase, median watch time per country, p95 page load time, "users in the top 10 percent of spend", median search frequency from a summary table (DataLemur "Median Google Search Frequency").
- Follow-ups: "Why median and not mean?" (skew and outliers; mean watch time is 27.1 here, above the median 24.5 because of a few long views). "How would you do this on a billion rows?" (approximate quantiles such as t-digest or `APPROX_QUANTILES`; exact medians need a full sort). "Is a change in the median significant?" (bootstrap or a quantile test; see [Choosing a test](#stats-choosing-a-test)).
- A strong answer sounds like: "I remove NULLs, number the rows in order with ROW_NUMBER and get n with COUNT OVER. I average the rows at positions (n + 1) / 2 and (n + 2) / 2 with integer division, which covers odd and even n. Per group I add PARTITION BY to both windows."

### Traps
- Keeping NULLs in the sort.
- Using `RANK()` instead of `ROW_NUMBER()`: ties share a rank, so the middle position may not exist.
- Decimal division in the positions (`(n + 1) / 2.0` gives 6.5, which matches no row).
- Forgetting `PARTITION BY` in one of the two windows when computing per group.
- Expanding a frequency table with a recursive CTE when a running sum is enough.
- Calling `NTILE` buckets exact percentiles: with ties or small `n` the buckets are only approximately equal.

### Complexity
Sorting is the cost: `O(n log n)` per query, or per partition. Exact percentiles cannot be done in one streaming pass with small memory, which is why big data engines use approximate algorithms.

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 23 (focus), reviewed on day 24.
- Related: [Window ranking](#sql-window-ranking), [Running totals](#sql-running-totals), [Top N](#sql-top-n), [Descriptive statistics](#stats-descriptive), [Choosing a test](#stats-choosing-a-test), [Heap: median from a data stream](#algo-heap), [pandas median and quantile](#sql-pandas-equivalents).
- LeetCode: [Find Median Given Frequency of Numbers](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-median-given-frequency-of-numbers/), [Median Employee Salary](https://leetcode.com/problems/median-employee-salary/), [Find Median from Data Stream](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-median-from-data-stream/) (the Python version).
- DataLemur: [Median Google Search Frequency](https://datalemur.com/questions/median-search-freq).
- Docs: [PostgreSQL ordered-set aggregates](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html#FUNCTIONS-ORDEREDSET-TABLE).

sections.title: Recursive CTEs (date spines, hierarchies, sequences)
sections.summary: Use to generate missing dates or numbers, and to walk a tree such as a referral chain or org chart.
sections.body:
### When to use it
Signals in the question:
- "include days with zero activity", "every day in the range, even if there were no views", "fill missing dates"
- "find the missing ids", "list all numbers from 1 to N", "hours of the day with no traffic"
- "all employees who report to the CEO directly or indirectly", "the full referral chain", "depth in the tree", "path from the root"
- "expand a row with quantity 3 into 3 rows"

What it is NOT: a fixed number of levels (manager and manager's manager) can be two [self joins](#sql-self-join). Recursion is for an unknown depth or for generating rows that do not exist in any table.

### Core idea
A recursive CTE has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`. The anchor member is a normal query that gives the starting rows. The recursive member refers to the CTE itself and produces the next rows from the rows of the previous step. The engine repeats the recursive member until it returns no new rows, so you need a stop condition (`WHERE n < 10`, or the tree simply ending). Tiny example: anchor `SELECT 1 AS n`, recursive step `SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 3`, result 1, 2, 3. Write `WITH RECURSIVE` (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8, SQLite). SQL Server writes only `WITH`, and Oracle supports both styles.

### Template
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (
  SELECT 1                       -- anchor: the first row
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums         -- recursive member: next row from the previous one
  WHERE n < 5                    -- stop condition
)
SELECT n FROM nums;
```

Result:

| n |
|---|
| 1 |
| 2 |
| 3 |
| 4 |
| 5 |


### Worked example 1: date spine to fill days with zero views
Question: "Daily views for every day from 2024-01-05 to 2024-01-13, with 0 on days without views, and a correct 3-day moving average."

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT DATE('2024-01-05')
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2024-01-13'
),
daily AS (
  SELECT DATE(event_ts) AS day, COUNT(*) AS views
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type = 'view'
  GROUP BY DATE(event_ts)
)
SELECT d.day,
       COALESCE(x.views, 0) AS views,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(x.views, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY d.day
             ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_3_days
FROM days AS d
LEFT JOIN daily AS x ON x.day = d.day
ORDER BY d.day;
```

Result:

| day | views | avg_3_days |
|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-05 | 3 | 3.0 |
| 2024-01-06 | 1 | 2.0 |
| 2024-01-07 | 1 | 1.67 |
| 2024-01-08 | 0 | 0.67 |
| 2024-01-09 | 0 | 0.33 |
| 2024-01-10 | 2 | 0.67 |
| 2024-01-11 | 1 | 1.0 |
| 2024-01-12 | 1 | 1.33 |
| 2024-01-13 | 1 | 1.0 |


The spine has every calendar day, the LEFT JOIN keeps days with no views, and `COALESCE` turns their NULL into 0. Now a `ROWS` frame is a true calendar window, which fixes the problem shown in [Running totals](#sql-running-totals) and [LAG and LEAD](#sql-lag-lead). In PostgreSQL you would usually write `generate_series(DATE '2024-01-05', DATE '2024-01-13', INTERVAL '1 day')` instead; BigQuery has `GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY`. Knowing the recursive version shows you can do it in any engine.

### Worked example 2: find what is missing (hours with no views)
Question: "Which hours of the day (0 to 23) never had a view in the `views` table?" This is the shape of LeetCode "Find the Missing IDs".

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE hours(h) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT h + 1 FROM hours WHERE h < 23
)
SELECT h AS hour_without_views
FROM hours
WHERE h NOT IN (SELECT CAST(strftime('%H', view_ts) AS INTEGER) FROM views)
ORDER BY h;
```

Result:

| hour_without_views |
|---|
| 0 |
| 1 |
| 2 |
| 3 |
| 4 |
| 5 |
| 6 |
| 11 |
| 14 |
| 15 |
| 16 |
| 17 |


`strftime('%H', ...)` returns text like `'09'`, so `CAST` it to an integer before comparing it with `h`. In PostgreSQL use `EXTRACT(HOUR FROM view_ts)`. `NOT IN` is safe here because the subquery has no NULLs; if it could, use `NOT EXISTS` or a LEFT JOIN with `IS NULL` (see [LEFT JOIN and NULLs](#sql-left-join-nulls)).

### Worked example 3: walk a tree (referral chains)
The made-up table `invites(user_id, invited_by)` stores who invited each user (NULL for organic signups):

```sql
SELECT i.user_id, u.username, i.invited_by
FROM invites AS i JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = i.user_id
ORDER BY i.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | username | invited_by |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | NULL |
| 2 | ben | 1 |
| 3 | chen | 1 |
| 4 | dana | 2 |
| 5 | eli | 4 |
| 6 | fay | NULL |


Question: "For every user, show the organic user at the top of their chain, their depth, and the full path."

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain(user_id, root_id, depth, path) AS (
  SELECT i.user_id, i.user_id, 0, CAST(u.username AS TEXT)
  FROM invites AS i
  JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = i.user_id
  WHERE i.invited_by IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT i.user_id, c.root_id, c.depth + 1, c.path || ' > ' || u.username
  FROM chain AS c
  JOIN invites AS i ON i.invited_by = c.user_id
  JOIN users AS u ON u.user_id = i.user_id
)
SELECT user_id, root_id, depth, path
FROM chain
ORDER BY root_id, depth, user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | root_id | depth | path |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | ana |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | ana > ben |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | ana > chen |
| 4 | 1 | 2 | ana > ben > dana |
| 5 | 1 | 3 | ana > ben > dana > eli |
| 6 | 6 | 0 | fay |


The anchor takes the roots (organic users). Each recursive step finds the users invited by the users found in the previous step, adds 1 to the depth and extends the path. It stops when a step finds no new invited users. `||` concatenates strings in SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL uses `CONCAT()`.

Follow-up: "How many users did each user bring in, directly or indirectly?" Start the anchor from every user and walk down:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE down(ancestor, descendant) AS (
  SELECT invited_by, user_id FROM invites WHERE invited_by IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.ancestor, i.user_id
  FROM down AS d
  JOIN invites AS i ON i.invited_by = d.descendant
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.username, COUNT(d.descendant) AS total_invited
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN down AS d ON d.ancestor = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.username
ORDER BY total_invited DESC, u.user_id;
```

Result:

| user_id | username | total_invited |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ana | 4 |
| 2 | ben | 2 |
| 4 | dana | 1 |
| 3 | chen | 0 |
| 5 | eli | 0 |
| 6 | fay | 0 |


Ana invited ben and chen directly, and through ben she also brought dana and, through dana, eli: 4 in total. This is LeetCode "All People Report to the Given Manager" in general form.

### Exam angle
- Typical asks: fill a calendar for a daily metric, list missing ids or dates, org chart depth, "all reports under a manager", category trees, bill of materials, expanding ranges into rows.
- Follow-ups: "What if the data has a cycle (A invited B, B invited A)?" (the recursion never stops; add `WHERE depth < 20` or keep the path and stop when the next id is already in it). "Recursion or generate_series?" (generate_series if the engine has it; recursion is portable). "Performance?" (each level is one join; deep trees on big tables are slow, so precompute a closure table).
- A strong answer sounds like: "I build a date spine with a recursive CTE from the start date, adding one day until the end date, then LEFT JOIN the daily counts and COALESCE to zero so missing days count in the moving average."

### Traps
- No stop condition: infinite recursion (SQLite and PostgreSQL run until they run out of memory or time; SQL Server stops at 100 levels by default, MySQL at `cte_max_recursion_depth` = 1000).
- `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`: it removes duplicates each step, which can hide bugs and is slower (it can also be a deliberate cycle guard; say so if you use it).
- Type mismatch between anchor and recursive member (for example a short text path in the anchor and a longer one later). Cast in the anchor, as in example 3.
- Comparing text dates with a different format (`'2024-1-5'` is not `'2024-01-05'`).
- Forgetting `COALESCE` after the LEFT JOIN to the spine.

### Complexity
A spine of `d` days costs `O(d)`. A tree walk costs one join per level: about `O(rows * depth)` with an index on the parent column (`invited_by`).

### Practice and links
- Practised on day 24 (focus).
- Related: [CTEs](#sql-cte), [Self joins](#sql-self-join), [Running totals](#sql-running-totals), [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands), [Trees in Python](#algo-trees), [Graphs: BFS and DFS](#algo-graphs-bfs-dfs).
- LeetCode: [Find the Missing IDs](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-missing-ids/), [All People Report to the Given Manager](https://leetcode.com/problems/all-people-report-to-the-given-manager/), [Find the Subtasks That Did Not Execute](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-subtasks-that-did-not-execute/).
- Docs: [SQLite WITH clause](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html), [PostgreSQL WITH queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html).

sections.title: SQL and pandas side by side
sections.summary: Use when the examiner says 'now do it in pandas' or when you think in SQL but must code in Python.
sections.body:
### When to use it
- The examiner says "now do the same in Python" after a SQL question, or the data round is in a notebook (Colab, CoderPad) instead of a SQL editor.
- You know the SQL answer and need the pandas words for it quickly.
- Product data questions in a Python coding round: sessionize a log, compute retention from a DataFrame, top creators by watch time (see [Data processing](#algo-data-processing)).

### Core idea
Most SQL maps to a few pandas tools. `WHERE` is a boolean mask, `JOIN` is `merge`, `GROUP BY` is `groupby(...).agg(...)`, and `HAVING` is a filter after the aggregation. Window functions split into two kinds. A window without `ORDER BY` (`SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY g)`) is `groupby(g).x.transform("sum")`: it keeps every row. A window with `ORDER BY` (`ROW_NUMBER`, `LAG`, running `SUM`) is "sort first, then `groupby` and `cumcount` / `shift` / `cumsum`". Pandas aligns results by index, so `df.assign(new=...)` puts each value back on its own row even after a sort.

Three differences cause most bugs:
1. **NULL versus NaN.** `groupby` drops NaN keys by default (`dropna=False` keeps them, like SQL `GROUP BY`). `merge` matches NaN keys with each other, while SQL never matches NULL = NULL.
2. **Booleans need `&`, `~` and brackets** around each condition, not `and`, `or`, `not`.
3. **Index.** After `groupby` the keys are in the index; call `reset_index()` to get columns back, or pass `as_index=False`.

### Setup used below
The same tables as the SQL examples, loaded from the notebook's SQLite database. `parse_dates` turns the text dates into pandas timestamps.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
# con = sqlite3.connect("ex.db")  # the notebook database that holds the example tables
users = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM users", con, parse_dates=["signup_date"])
videos = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM videos", con, parse_dates=["upload_date"])
views = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM views", con, parse_dates=["view_ts"])
events = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events", con, parse_dates=["event_ts"])
events_raw = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM events_raw", con)
user_devices = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM user_devices", con, parse_dates=["updated_at"])
print(views.dtypes)
```

Output:

```text
view_id               int64
user_id               int64
video_id              int64
view_ts      datetime64[ns]
watch_sec           float64
dtype: object
```


`watch_sec` became `float64` because it has a NULL: NaN is a float, so an integer column with missing values turns into floats (or use the nullable `"Int64"` type).

### Side-by-side table
Every row below was run on the example data, and the SQL and pandas results were checked to be equal.

**Select and filter**

| Operation | SQL | pandas |
|---|---|---|
| Pick columns | `SELECT user_id, country FROM users` | `users[["user_id", "country"]]` |
| Filter rows (AND) | `SELECT * FROM users WHERE country = 'US' AND signup_date >= '2024-02-01'` | `users[(users.country == "US") & (users.signup_date >= "2024-02-01")]` |
| IN list | `SELECT * FROM users WHERE country IN ('US', 'KR')` | `users[users.country.isin(["US", "KR"])]` |
| IS NULL | `SELECT * FROM users WHERE country IS NULL` | `users[users.country.isna()]` |
| LIKE 'd%' | `SELECT * FROM users WHERE username LIKE 'd%'` | `users[users.username.str.startswith("d")]` |
| ORDER BY ... LIMIT | `SELECT * FROM views ORDER BY watch_sec DESC LIMIT 3` | `views.sort_values("watch_sec", ascending=False).head(3)` |
| DISTINCT | `SELECT DISTINCT category FROM videos` | `videos[["category"]].drop_duplicates()` |
| CASE WHEN | `SELECT view_id, CASE WHEN watch_sec >= 30 THEN 'long' ELSE 'short' END AS kind FROM views` | `views.assign(kind=np.where(views.watch_sec >= 30, "long", "short"))[["view_id", "kind"]]` |
| COALESCE | `SELECT view_id, COALESCE(watch_sec, 0) AS w FROM views` | `views.assign(w=views.watch_sec.fillna(0))[["view_id", "w"]]` |
| LOWER(TRIM(x)) | `SELECT LOWER(TRIM(event_type)) AS t FROM events_raw` | `events_raw.event_type.str.strip().str.lower()` |

**Aggregate**

| Operation | SQL | pandas |
|---|---|---|
| COUNT(DISTINCT) | `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events` | `events.user_id.nunique()` |
| GROUP BY with several aggregates | `SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(duration_sec) AS avg_dur FROM videos GROUP BY category` | `videos.groupby("category").agg(n=("video_id", "size"), avg_dur=("duration_sec", "mean")).reset_index()` |
| HAVING | `SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM views GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3` | `views.groupby("user_id").size().reset_index(name="n").query("n >= 3")` |
| Conditional rate AVG(CASE) | `SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN watch_sec >= 30 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) FROM views` | `(views.watch_sec >= 30).mean()` |
| Percent of total | `SELECT category, 1.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () AS share FROM videos GROUP BY category` | `videos.category.value_counts(normalize=True)` |
| Group by month | `SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', event_ts) AS month, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY month` | `events.groupby(events.event_ts.dt.to_period("M")).size()` |

**Join**

| Operation | SQL | pandas |
|---|---|---|
| INNER JOIN | `SELECT w.view_id, v.category FROM views w JOIN videos v ON v.video_id = w.video_id` | `views.merge(videos, on="video_id")[["view_id", "category"]]` |
| LEFT JOIN, count with zeros | `SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(w.view_id) AS n FROM users u LEFT JOIN views w ON w.user_id = u.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id` | `users.merge(views, on="user_id", how="left").groupby("user_id").view_id.count().reset_index(name="n")` |
| Anti join (never viewed) | `SELECT u.user_id FROM users u LEFT JOIN views w ON w.user_id = u.user_id WHERE w.user_id IS NULL` | `users.loc[~users.user_id.isin(views.user_id), ["user_id"]]` |
| Semi join (IN subquery) | `SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM events WHERE event_type = 'like')` | `users[users.user_id.isin(events.loc[events.event_type == "like", "user_id"])]` |
| Self join: pairs on the same video | `SELECT DISTINCT a.user_id AS u1, b.user_id AS u2 FROM views a JOIN views b ON a.video_id = b.video_id AND a.user_id < b.user_id` | `views.merge(views, on="video_id").query("user_id_x < user_id_y")[["user_id_x", "user_id_y"]].drop_duplicates()` |
| UNION ALL / UNION | `SELECT user_id FROM views UNION SELECT creator_id FROM videos` | `pd.concat([views.user_id, videos.creator_id]).drop_duplicates()` |

**Window**

| Operation | SQL | pandas |
|---|---|---|
| ROW_NUMBER per group | `SELECT view_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY view_ts) AS rn FROM views` | `views.assign(rn=views.sort_values("view_ts").groupby("user_id").cumcount() + 1)[["view_id", "rn"]]` |
| RANK (ties share a rank) | `SELECT view_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY video_id ORDER BY watch_sec DESC) AS r FROM views WHERE watch_sec IS NOT NULL` | `views.dropna(subset=["watch_sec"]).assign(r=lambda d: d.groupby("video_id").watch_sec.rank(method="min", ascending=False))[["view_id", "r"]]` |
| Top 1 per group | `SELECT user_id, view_id FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY watch_sec DESC) AS rn FROM views) WHERE rn = 1` | `views.sort_values("watch_sec", ascending=False).groupby("user_id").head(1)[["user_id", "view_id"]]` |
| LAG | `SELECT view_id, LAG(view_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY view_ts) AS prev_ts FROM views` | `views.assign(prev_ts=views.sort_values("view_ts").groupby("user_id").view_ts.shift(1))[["view_id", "prev_ts"]]` |
| Running total (NULL as 0) | `SELECT view_id, SUM(watch_sec) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY view_ts ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS run FROM views` | `views.sort_values("view_ts").assign(run=lambda d: d.watch_sec.fillna(0).groupby(d.user_id).cumsum())[["view_id", "run"]]` |
| Group total on every row | `SELECT view_id, SUM(watch_sec) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS user_total FROM views` | `views.assign(user_total=views.groupby("user_id").watch_sec.transform("sum"))[["view_id", "user_total"]]` |

**Clean and reshape**

| Operation | SQL | pandas |
|---|---|---|
| Keep latest row per key | `SELECT user_id, device FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, device) AS rn FROM user_devices) WHERE rn = 1` | `user_devices.sort_values(["updated_at", "device"], ascending=[False, True]).drop_duplicates("user_id")[["user_id", "device"]]` |
| Pivot (CASE WHEN per column) | `SELECT user_id, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'like' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS likes, SUM(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS views FROM events GROUP BY user_id` | `pd.crosstab(events.user_id, events.event_type)[["like", "view"]]` |
| Median and p90 | see [Median and percentiles](#sql-median-percentiles) | `views.watch_sec.median(), views.watch_sec.quantile(0.9)` |

Notes on the table:
- `query("n >= 3")` is the pandas `HAVING`. You can also write `df[df.n >= 3]`.
- `sort_values` puts NaN last in both directions by default (`na_position="last"`). SQLite treats NULL as the smallest value, so it comes first in `ASC` and last in `DESC`; PostgreSQL does the opposite. Say how you handle NULLs when you sort.
- `rank(method="min")` is SQL `RANK`, `method="dense"` is `DENSE_RANK`, `method="first"` is like `ROW_NUMBER` (ties by position). `rank` gives NaN for NaN values, which is why the `RANK` row drops NULLs on both sides.
- `transform` returns one value per original row (a window), `agg` returns one row per group (a `GROUP BY`).
- For the running total the SQL `SUM` skips NULL; in pandas `cumsum` leaves NaN at that row, so fill with 0 first.

### Worked example 1: D1 and D7 retention by signup month
Same question as [Retention](#sql-retention) example 1.

```python
active = (events.assign(day=events.event_ts.dt.normalize())[["user_id", "day"]]
          .drop_duplicates())
active_idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_frame(active)
last_day = active.day.max()

def dn_flag(n):
    target = users.signup_date + pd.Timedelta(days=n)
    hit = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([users.user_id, target]).isin(active_idx)
    return pd.Series(hit.astype(float), index=users.index).where(target <= last_day)  # NaN = not observable yet

ret = users.assign(cohort=users.signup_date.dt.to_period("M"), d1=dn_flag(1), d7=dn_flag(7))
print((ret.groupby("cohort")[["d1", "d7"]].mean() * 100).round(1))
```

Output:

```text
           d1     d7
cohort              
2024-01  50.0  100.0
2024-02  50.0   50.0
2024-03   0.0    NaN
```


The numbers match the SQL result. `where(target <= last_day)` plays the role of the SQL `CASE ... THEN NULL` for immature cohorts, and `mean()` skips NaN just like `AVG`. Fay has no events but is in `users`, so she is in the denominator.

### Worked example 2: longest streak (gaps and islands)
Same question as [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands) example 1.

```python
d = active.sort_values(["user_id", "day"]).copy()
gap = d.groupby("user_id").day.diff()                 # NaT on each user's first row
d["island"] = gap.ne(pd.Timedelta(days=1)).cumsum()   # new island when the gap is not 1 day
streaks = d.groupby(["user_id", "island"]).day.agg(["min", "max", "size"])
print(streaks.groupby("user_id")["size"].max())
```

Output:

```text
user_id
1    3
2    4
3    1
4    3
5    1
Name: size, dtype: int64
```


`diff()` is `day - LAG(day)`. A new island starts on each user's first row (NaT is "not equal" to 1 day) and after each gap, and `cumsum()` of that flag is the island id. This is the flag and running sum trick; the difference trick (`day - row_number`) also works but is longer in pandas.

### Worked example 3: sessions with a 30-minute rule
Same question as [Gaps and islands](#sql-gaps-islands) example 2.

```python
e = events.sort_values(["user_id", "event_ts"]).copy()
gap = e.groupby("user_id").event_ts.diff()
e["session_id"] = (gap.isna() | (gap > pd.Timedelta(minutes=30))).astype(int).groupby(e.user_id).cumsum()
summary = e.groupby("user_id").agg(sessions=("session_id", "nunique"), events=("event_ts", "size"))
summary["events_per_session"] = (summary.events / summary.sessions).round(2)
print(summary)
```

### Worked example 4: daily views with missing days and a 3-day moving average
Same question as [Recursive CTE](#sql-recursive-cte) example 1 (the date spine).

```python
daily = (events[events.event_type == "view"]
         .groupby(events.event_ts.dt.normalize()).size())
spine = pd.date_range("2024-01-05", "2024-01-13", freq="D")
daily = daily.reindex(spine, fill_value=0)            # the date spine plus COALESCE(..., 0)
out = pd.DataFrame({"views": daily,
                    "avg_3_days": daily.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean().round(2)})
print(out)
```

```text
2024-01-08      0        0.67
```

`reindex` with a full `date_range` is the pandas date spine. `rolling(3, min_periods=1)` is `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, including the shorter windows at the start. ### Exam angle
- Common requests: "Write it in pandas", "Now the data does not fit in memory" (filter and aggregate in SQL first, or use chunked reading, Polars, DuckDB or Spark), "Which would you use in production?" (SQL close to the warehouse for heavy aggregation, pandas for the last mile and modelling).
- A strong answer sounds like: "A window with ORDER BY is sort, groupby and then cumcount, shift or cumsum, and a window without ORDER BY is groupby transform. I use assign so the results align back on the original index."
- Speed matters in a live round: know `groupby().agg(name=(col, func))`, `merge(how=...)`, `transform`, `shift`, `cumsum`, `rank`, `pivot_table`, `melt`, `drop_duplicates(keep=...)` without looking them up. See the [pandas cheat sheet](#cheat-pandas).

### Traps
- `and` / `or` instead of `&` / `|`, or missing brackets: `df[df.a > 1 & df.b < 2]` is wrong because `&` binds before `>`.
- Forgetting to sort before `shift`, `cumsum` or `cumcount`: the "previous row" is then the previous row in file order.
- Chained assignment (`df[df.x > 0]["y"] = 1`) changes a copy. Use `df.loc[mask, "y"] = 1`.
- `count()` skips NaN, `size()` does not. They are `COUNT(col)` and `COUNT(*)`.
- `merge` on columns with duplicate keys multiplies rows (the same fan-out as in SQL). Check with `validate="one_to_one"` or `"many_to_one"`.
- `groupby` drops NaN keys unless `dropna=False`, so eli (country NaN) disappears from a country breakdown.
- `value_counts()` also drops NaN unless `dropna=False`.

### Complexity
pandas operations are vectorized and in memory: `groupby` and `merge` are hash based, about `O(n)`; `sort_values` is `O(n log n)`. Python loops over rows (`iterrows`, `apply` with a Python function) are 10 to 100 times slower; avoid them in exams unless the logic really needs a loop.
